The programme begins today at Target Supermarket in Yong Peng, Batu Pahat, the Benut multipurpose hall in Pontian, the Kota Tinggi Tourism and Transformation Centre and the IOI Mall Kulai field on November 7 and 8.
56791ba0ab009ead: Machado returns to a hopeful, cautious nation
Originally published on Global Voices
María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile. The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country. She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro. Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S. President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:
Estoy aquí. Con ustedes
— María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026
I am here. With you all.

Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans. Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.
A different country

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.

Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process. Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.
The crowd waited for hours for Maria Corina Machado's arrival to the capital city. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Yet, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures. Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different. There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.

People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time. After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.

Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her. She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen. On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.

At one point, two patrols from the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) passed by. The people closest to the highway lane began shouting at them, “Get out, get out!” but no one blocked their path or touched their doors or windows and the patrols continued on their way. Known as Venezuela’s political police, the DGCIM was one of the bodies singled out for 2024’s repressive post-election measures, in which more than 2,300 people were detained.
New uncertainties

Asked about the possible aftermaths of Machado’s return, caravan participants shared differing perspectives. Veterinarian Marianna Torres had no doubts about the order of things: Venezuela must have presidential elections, and soon, but not with the same electoral institutions that have permitted electoral fraud in the past. For her, all branches of power are corrupt and must be cleaned up before any election.

She also urged people looking at Venezuela from the outside to stop listening solely to politicians and pay attention to what “everyday Venezuelans” — the ones who know there are still political prisoners, human rights violations, and government authoritarian control — are saying.

Gabriela Santander, a publicist and activist for the Encuentro Ciudadano party, thought almost the opposite regarding the timeline. Stressing that she had been waiting for this day for months, since before Machado left, she believes that going to vote now, without an independent electoral arbiter or an impartial Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ), would be falling into a trap. Her deadline is concrete: if a new Electoral National Center is not in place by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the time to put on pressure will arrive.

Santander suspects that behind Machado’s return — which she believes could not have happened without Washington's approval — are agreements that no one has disclosed, especially since Rubio confirmed that his government had negotiated her return with the interim government “many weeks ago.” What Santander noticed the night of the caravan, however, was something more important: people had been on the highway for more than four hours and authorities had not tried to detain them.

Attorney Joyffer Briceño took a pragmatic view of the situation. While he sees Machado as the leader of those who want to restore the country’s institutions, he does not mistake emotion for change. “Those who hold power today are the same ones who were part of the crisis for years,” he explained. “I want something less abstract than an economic growth figure; I want the improvement to be felt in the pockets of every Venezuelan.”

For José Gregorio Rodríguez Cham, Machado’s arrival carries a different weight. His father, Julio Rodríguez Salazar, is a political prisoner, so he attended the event with other relatives to continue demanding the release of the 322 political prisoners who, according to Foro Penal, remain detained. He believes that new elections would be different because of the oversight of the United States, but he does not deny that the repressive apparatus in Venezuela remains intact, and that dismantling it will take time. What he years for in the coming months are elections and freedom, starting with that of his family.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Raquel Bugallo, a merchant in Caracas, remains somewhat suspicious of outside help. She believes that the international humanitarian aid Venezuela expected was overshadowed by economic interests, and that oil has been both Venezuela’s greatest wealth and “worst curse.” While she didn’t reject Rubio's call for understanding among all sectors, she did attach a condition: finding common ground, as long as the country can move forward. Her message to the international community was the shortest of the night: “If you are not going to help us, don’t get in our way.”

The day after Machado’s return, Delcy Rodríguez quipped that “the show could have been avoided.” Meanwhile, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights reminded the Venezuelan state of its obligation to guarantee the life, integrity, and political rights of the leader. Between November 11 and 15, the dialogue table will meet again, for the first time with Machado inside the country.

In the meantime, Venezuelans can savour the feeling of having spent hours on the streets without that familiar fear of repression. While repressive bodies were still present, passing in patrols through the crowd, on October 25, 2026, with Machado waving from the back of a pickup truck, the people stared back at them and told them to go, which must have felt something like progress.
Written by Óscar Calles
dde87bf8d87f5b30: SINGAPORE, Nov 6 — Singapore police have warned of large crowds in Little India during the Deepavali celebrations, especially on the eve of the festival on Nov 7, and urged motorists to use alternative routes, The Straits Times reported.
In an advisory issued today, the police said heavy foot and vehicular traffic was expected along Serangoon Road during the period.

The pedestrian crossing at Birch Road, in front of Angullia Mosque, will be closed from 4pm on Nov 7 until 4am the next day, with pedestrians directed to alternative crossings near Kitchener Link or Baboo Lane.
The crossing at Campbell Lane may also be shut if required, with alternatives available near Sungei Road or Dunlop Street.
Auxiliary police officers and directional signboards will be deployed to manage crowd movement, the report said.
Public drinking is banned in Little India and Geylang, both Liquor Control Zones, from 10.30pm on Nov 6 to 7am on Nov 10.
The report said, first-time offenders face fines of up to S$1,500, while repeat offenders may be fined up to S$3,000, jailed for up to four and a half months, or both.
Retailers caught selling alcohol outside permitted trading hours risk losing their liquor licences, the police said.

The police also warned against the illegal import, possession and discharge of fireworks, saying they would take strict enforcement action against offenders as such acts endanger the public and their property.
A total of 45 people were investigated for fireworks-related offences in 2025, The Straits Times reported.
Individuals convicted face up to three years’ jail and a fine of up to S$50,000, while entities can be fined up to S$100,000.
Misusing sparklers, such as bundling them together and lighting them at once, is also an offence punishable by up to a year’s jail, a fine of up to S$5,000, or both.
Those who hurt others while misusing sparklers can be jailed for up to three years, fined, or both.
The public was also advised to stay vigilant and keep their belongings secure, including wearing bags across the front and keeping them zipped.
ea8c3744679ca428: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Canadian R&B superstar The Weeknd’s After Hours Til Dawn (AHTD) tour is officially the highest-grossing tour by a male artist, grossing over US$1.3 billion (RM5.4 billion), according to Live Nation Entertainment.

The AHTD tour, which wrapped up with its final show last night at the TM National Stadium in Bukit Jalil, surpassed the previous record held by Sir Elton John’s Farewell Yellow Brick Road tour, which grossed US$939.1 million.

This also makes The Weeknd, whose real name is Abel Tesfaye, one of the few artists in the world with concert tours surpassing the billion-dollar mark, joining Taylor Swift (US$2.07 billion) and Coldplay (US$1.52 billion).

The Asian leg of the AHTD tour, initially announced with 11 dates, was subsequently expanded to 17 shows amid overwhelming demand, including an additional night in Kuala Lumpur, three nights in Bangkok, four in Hong Kong and further dates across other markets.
According to a statement by tour promoter Live Nation, the AHTD stadium tour spanned 176 shows across 67 cities, 30 countries and five continents, selling more than nine million tickets.
In 2026 alone, the tour sold more than three million tickets and grossed over US$500 million.
In July, the tour topped Billboard’s monthly Boxscore chart, grossing more than US$120 million and selling nearly 900,000 tickets in a single month.
The Weeknd has also donated US$8.5 million to the XO Humanitarian Fund and Global Citizen, supporting global hunger relief and access to quality education for children worldwide.
The XO Humanitarian Fund is a charitable initiative launched by The Weeknd in partnership with the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) to support global hunger-relief efforts.
In 2026 alone, US$3 million has been raised for the WFP and Global Citizen.

This year’s contributions to Global Citizen will support a new campaign aimed at breaking down barriers faced by women and girls in health, education and economic opportunities, while securing commitments to empower them to reach their full potential.

Meanwhile, The Weeknd has also broken multiple records across China’s major music streaming platforms with his surprise single Hong Kong, which debuted on October 24 during the opening night of his four-show run at Kai Tak Stadium in Hong Kong.

The single, which samples Cantopop icon Faye Wong, achieved the biggest first-day debut for a non-Mandarin song in the past five years across streams, likes, saves, comments and shares on NetEase Cloud Music.

The Weeknd also became the first international artist in five years to reach No. 1 on all three major charts on the platform, including Hot Song, Surging and New Music, on the song’s release day on October 31.
He also broke a similar record on QQ Music, where the track earned the biggest debut ever for a Western male artist across streams, saves, comments and shares.
This made The Weeknd the first Western artist in 2026 to top all three major charts on release day.
95b5b60b3a171370: HONG KONG: A leading Macau democrat was jailed for 12.5 years on Friday on charges of subversion, in the China-ruled gambling hub's first known national security trial, local broadcaster TDM reported.
Au Kam San, 69, was arrested in July 2025 for collusion with foreign forces to endanger national security and tried behind closed doors on Sept 16 and 18, TDM said.

Au is one of Macau's most prominent democratic campaigners who served for nearly two decades as a lawmaker in the former Portuguese colony. His lawyer, who was appointed by the court, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

His sentencing comes a day after Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong, who became the global face of the financial hub's pro-democracy movement, was sentenced to 10 years in jail on ​a charge of collusion with foreign entities under the city's national security law.

Macau's Court of First Instance found Au guilty of subversion of state power, establishing links with foreign groups or individuals to commit activities endangering national security and violation of secrecy.

"Although the defendant is a first-time offender and has admitted to a significant portion of the criminal acts, the degree of intent was extremely high, and both the unlawfulness of the conduct and the potential consequences are exceptionally grave," TDM said, citing the court.
The court acquitted Au on two additional counts of subversion due to insufficient evidence.

The applicable range for Au's cumulative sentence was between 11 years and 3 months and 19 years and 6 months of imprisonment, TDM said. "Following deliberation, the court imposed a single, consolidated sentence of 12 years and 6 months of imprisonment."

Through the years, Au had championed democratic reforms and civil society initiatives in the tiny enclave that returned from Portuguese to Chinese rule in 1999 -- two years after the neighbouring former British colony of Hong Kong was handed back to China.

Human Rights Watch said the proceedings were "marred by violations of due process" and the sentence handed down by the Macao government "sends a chilling message to all peaceful critics in the territory."
Pro-democracy voices have faced an intense crackdown in the China-ruled territories since Hong Kong's 2019 protest movement.

In February, media tycoon Jimmy Lai, Hong Kong's most vocal China critic, was jailed for 20 years for collusion with foreign forces and sedition following a landmark ​trial that sparked international criticism.

c5e48eab8233c409: SINGAPORE: Singapore Airlines, long a benchmark for premium travel, is spending more than S$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) to upgrade long-haul seats and provide larger double-bed suites to compete with rivals that are pouring money into high-end cabins.
The airline on Friday unveiled new cabins in all four travel classes in the biggest and most comprehensive overhaul in its history, with the new seats due from the second half of 2027.

In first class, centre seats convert into what Singapore Airlines calls the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Business class gets sliding privacy doors for the first time on the airline, alongside a fully flat bed.

The launch comes as carriers globally such as Air France, British Airways and United Airlines pour billions into premium travel despite industry-wide delays in production and certification of new seats.
Surging fuel costs have squeezed margins and pushed up fares, deterring some more cost-conscious economy passengers, although premium travel has remained relatively resilient.

The investment "underpins our long-standing commitment to continually raise the bar of premium air travel," Yeoh Phee Teik, Singapore Airlines' senior vice-president customer experience, said at a briefing on Wednesday.
The Singapore Airlines programme covers 72 aircraft, a mix of Airbus A350-900s being retrofitted and Boeing 777-9 jets on order that together will comprise the majority of its long-haul fleet.
The cabins were originally designed for the 777-9, which is expected to become Singapore Airlines' new long-haul flagship as the A380, which offers smaller double beds, eventually retires.
But the 777-9's entry into service has slipped for years, which Singapore Airlines chief commercial officer Lee Lik Hsin told Reuters had led the carrier to widen the programme to its A350s.

He said the S$2 billion-plus investment included a S$1.1 billion A350 refurbishment plan announced in 2024 and was funded from the airline's strong cash balance, which stood at S$9.1 billion as of end-June.

Most of the investment goes to premium cabins because business and first-class seats cost far more per unit than economy seats, Lee said, with the carrier setting no spending ceiling and planning to keep investing when appropriate to maintain its market leadership.
"Our competitive advantage doesn't derive from aircraft cabin product alone," he said. "It is the hard product, the soft service, the operational excellence. And...it is our people."

David Flynn, editor-in-chief of industry publication Executive Traveller, said the new first class with a unique curved cabin design that borrowed space from the aisles to add personal space to each suite ranked among the world's best.

"Business class represent a solid and much-needed catch up to the competition, rather than a mighty leap ahead," he said. "It's hard to top Qatar's business class Qsuite, let alone the next-gen version coming in 2027, but in features and usability, Singapore Airlines looks to have Emirates and arguably Cathay beat here."
Delays and certification

The unveiling arrives against a backdrop of persistent delays. Boeing first targeted 777-9 deliveries around 2020 but repeated certification setbacks, engine issues, the pandemic and tighter oversight by the US Federal Aviation Administration have pushed that to 2027, with Lufthansa expected to be the launch operator.
Lee said slippage on its A350 refurbishment plan and the 777-9 seating were both driven by certification issues.
"The seats are certified on the 777-9, but the 777-9 aeroplane itself is not certified, and the seats have not yet been certified on the A350," he said.
The A350 certification delay had pushed back their introduction by about half a year, he added.
As airlines design more premium offerings with bespoke features that regulators need to ensure meet stringent crash-safety standards, seat certification has become a bottleneck across the industry.
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg last week told investors that deliveries of its 787 Dreamliners had been affected by seat certification challenges.
0d4fbb271bee2b6f: SINGAPORE, Nov 6 — Singapore Airlines (SIA) will start installing its next-generation first- and business-class seats on its Airbus A350-900 fleet from the second half of 2027, slightly later than its earlier target of the first quarter of 2027, The Straits Times reported.
SIA said industry-wide supply constraints and a delay in certifying the new seats had pushed back the upgrades, according to the Singapore daily.

The first A350-900 long-haul aircraft with the new seats was originally expected to carry passengers in the second quarter of 2026, with the ultra-long-range version of the A350-900 to follow in 2027.
The new economy and premium economy seats will be fitted only on SIA’s new Boeing 777-9 aircraft, the report said.
The Straits Times reported that the seat upgrades for the entire A350 fleet are part of a S$2 billion revamp across all cabin classes and are scheduled to be completed by 2030.
Covering 72 aircraft in total, it is the airline’s biggest investment in cabin products to date.
The wider refresh also includes updated dining menus and enhanced in-flight entertainment systems.
SIA last overhauled the business-class seats on its Airbus A380s in 2017, when it also redesigned its Suites, the A380’s equivalent of a first-class cabin. — AFP
3a0a8f90d692a33f: KUALA LUMPUR: The High Court here has issued a house arrest order for Najib Razak, his lawyer said following the settlement of the former prime minister’s RM50 million fine.
Umno earlier said it had settled the fine imposed on Najib, its former president, after collecting enough funds through its donation drive launched in September.
"What I can confirm at this stage is that... Umno has paid the RM50 million to the High Court," Najib’s lawyer, Farhan Shafee, told reporters here.
"As a result, pursuant to the royal order, the court has issued the house arrest order, which we have received.
"There are still further processes that need to be completed, so I will not be taking any questions for now. I am now heading to Kajang prison to deliver the order."
Najib was jailed in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million in SRC International funds.
He was sentenced to 12 years' jail and fined RM210 million.
In January 2024, a royal pardon halved his prison sentence and reduced his fine to RM50 million.

In September this year, the current Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.
The release was subject to Najib paying the RM50 million fine and complying with other conditions.
e733f23ac0b5dc98: SYDNEY, Nov 6 — An elderly woman wounded in last year’s mass shooting at Bondi Beach has died from complications linked to her injuries, a Jewish community group said today.
A father-and-son duo are accused of killing 15 people and wounding dozens more in an antisemitic attack at the famous beach on December 14 last year.
Eva Geller, 90, died in hospital almost 11 months after she was shot while attending a Hanukkah event, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry said in a statement.
“It is reported that she developed an infection as a result of her wounds and was admitted to hospital, where she passed away overnight,” the group said.
Geller had been repeatedly hospitalised in the wake of the attack, local media reported.
New South Wales Police said they were speaking with the coroner and awaiting further advice.
Alleged shooter Naveed Akram remains in custody and has been charged with 15 murders, committing a terrorist act, and dozens of other serious offences.
His father Sajid Akram, 50, was shot and killed by police during the December 14 attack. — AFP
2943260cadee1982: HONG KONG: China and Hong Kong stocks fell on Friday as a Nasdaq-led tech rout rippled across Asia and fuelled fears the AI boom is losing steam, although bargain hunting helped pare losses in mainland markets buoyed by Beijing's market-supporting measures.
China's blue-chip CSI300 Index dropped 1.5% by the midday break, but remained on track to snap a 12-week-long losing streak. The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.1%.
The tech-heavy selloff was initially more severe. Both the tech-focused Star 50 Index and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index was down 1%, while the Hang Seng Artificial Intelligence Index tumbled 4%.

Overnight, the Nasdaq posted its steepest one-day drop since April 2025, wiping trillions of dollars off market value as investors fretted that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could bring tighter scrutiny of the AI sector.
The risk-off mood spilled over to Asia in early hours, with South Korea's Kospi plunging more than 8% at one point and Japan's Nikkei falling 5%.
Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai, said the overnight slump in US tech stocks meant the logic behind the AI-driven rally had crumbled.
"The US stock market has been the standard-bearer and backbone of the global AI bull run. Now that backbone has snapped. Can AI bull markets elsewhere hold up on their own?" he said.

Chinese AI hardware stocks with significant exposure to the US market were among the hardest hit. Zhongji Innolight, which makes optical transceivers for data centres and generates most of its revenue in America, slumped 8% to a one-year low. Rival Eoptolink Technology tanked 7%.
AI software firms also came under pressure, with Zhipu sinking as much as 15.4% amid concerns that a broader AI backlash could threaten the timing of Anthropic's IPO.
Jason Hsu, founder and chairman of Rayliant Global Advisors, said China's sentiment-driven stock market was heavily influenced by AI stock performance in the US.

Technology stocks carry significant weight in China's stock market and "what people are really watching closely is whether AI in the United States is a bubble," he said, adding that any signs of a bubble bursting in the US "obviously will affect the Chinese market".

Still, early panic selling drew in bargain hunters, helping trim losses in a market that remains on course for weekly gains after Beijing rolled out support measures and reiterated its commitment to preventing systemic risks.
"I don't think China can completely escape the fallout from Wall Street, especially with selling this aggressive," said Pepperstone strategist Dilin Wu.

"But I'd be careful about treating China's entire AI supply chain as one trade," she said, adding growth in AI chip players like Huawei and Cambricon are mainly driven by China's push for technological self-reliance.
"When investors rush to cut risk, even good companies get sold."
6ef467c3f294236a: WASHINGTON: US nonfarm payrolls likely picked up in October, but an anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3.0% for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years would reinforce the view that the labour market was not a source of inflation.

The Labor Department's closely watched employment report on Friday is also expected to show the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.2% last month, with a high probability it may have slipped to 4.1%. Historically low layoffs and a recent jump in job openings have raised the prospect of labour market tightening.

But economists and Federal Reserve officials have maintained that the labour market poses no inflation risk. Some economists have argued that a shrinking supply of workers amid an immigration crackdown and retirements is the primary driver of the relatively low unemployment rate.

"We have got a jobs market which isn't generating wage growth in any meaningful way. That really should help to dampen medium-term price pressures because the biggest cost input for corporate America is labour," said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING. "Weak wage growth should the give Fed some confidence that over the medium term, inflation will continue trending towards target."

Nonfarm payrolls likely increased by 65,000 jobs last month, a Reuters survey of economists predicted, after being restricted to a 29,000 gain in September because of a calendar quirk related to a late Labor Day holiday. Estimates ranged from 35,000 to 125,000 jobs.
October payrolls could also miss expectations, with some economists noting seasonal factors, used by the government to strip out seasonal fluctuations from the data, were unfavorable for the month.

Employment gains have averaged 68,000 jobs per month this year. Economists say the economy needs to create at least 40,000 per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population. The so-called breakeven rate has declined from roughly 150,000 in 2024 because of the smaller labor force.

Payroll gains have lagged economic growth, with gross domestic product increasing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, fueled by strong consumer spending and businesses aggressively investing in artificial intelligence. Economists said employers likely overhired after the COVID pandemic, and some businesses were probably uncertain about their staffing needs as they incorporated AI into their operations.

They said uncertainty stemming from the US-Israel war with Iran, which has raised energy prices, was also making employers hesitant to increase headcount. Limited opportunities have made job hopping harder, curbing wage growth.
It is also difficult for young adults, recent college graduates and some unemployed people to find work.

Disenchantment over the economy as well as anger over the Middle East conflict, now in its ninth month, cost President Donald Trump's Republican Party control of Congress, with Democrats performing strongly in this week's midterm elections.

"Job security remains elevated for workers already employed, while opportunities for job seekers and job switchers have become more limited," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. "More broadly, the economy has shifted toward a job-light expansion, as investment tilts toward technology and firms increasingly meet solid demand by relying more on their existing workforce, as reflected in firmer hours worked."

Average hourly earnings are forecast to have increased 0.3% in October after edging up 0.1% in September. Wages are expected to have advanced 2.9% in the 12 months through October. That would be the first year-on-year increase below 3% since May 2021 and a slowdown from a 3.0% gain in September.
While that would highlight the disinflationary impulse from the labor market, it would illustrate the further erosion of household incomes, already pressured by inflation.
Income at the disposal of households after adjusting for inflation and taxes fell in September.

Economists expect consumer spending and the broader economy will slow down in the fourth quarter and into 2027. They continued to expect the US central bank to raise interest rates in December, though some believed benign wage pressure could limit the number of rate hikes next year. The Fed last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."
Next Tuesday's consumer inflation report for October could offer more clues on the course of monetary policy in early 2027.

"The labour market is not too hot, not too cold," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "So, the Fed has nothing to worry about when it comes to the labor situation."
b91e3f9178b5fd8f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Umno has completed all payment processes to the Kuala Lumpur High Court for the RM50 million fine imposed on former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak, the party announced today.

Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said that the Najib Razak Solidarity Fund launched on September 18 had reached its collection target and was sufficient, according to the statement shared on his Facebook page.
“Umno has completed all payment processes to the Kuala Lumpur High Court this morning,” he said.
He also announced that the party had officially closed the special account established for public donations.
“Umno hereby officially closes the special Najib Razak Solidarity Fund account and no longer needs crowdfunding for this purpose,” he said.
Asyraf Wajdi expressed the party’s gratitude to Allah and thanked Umno members nationwide and the public who had contributed since the fund’s launch.
The statement did not disclose the total amount collected.
Najib, 73, has been at Kajang Prison since August 23, 2022, after the Federal Court upheld his conviction over the misappropriation of RM42 million from SRC International Sdn Bhd.
His original sentence was 12 years’ jail and a RM210 million fine, which the Federal Territories Pardons Board reduced in January 2024 to six years and RM50 million.

Sultan Ibrahim, the King of Malaysia, granted Najib a conditional pardon on September 18, permitting him to serve the rest of his term under house arrest until August 23, 2028, provided the fine and other conditions are met.
cba167adf7fdddb4: LOS ANGELES, Nov 6 — The manager of US country music legend Dolly Parton dropped a civil lawsuit against the singer’s nephew on Thursday, US media reported, after a row enveloped the late musician’s estate.

The lawsuit filed in September by Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell accused her nephew, Bryan Seaver, of attempting to extort money from the estate, which includes an amusement park, a hotel and a soon-to-be-opened museum.
Seaver, who broke the news of the singer’s death at age 80 in an emotional video in August, had provided security for Parton for years but was abruptly fired, according to TMZ.
Court filings alleged that Seaver sent threats including a text message warning he would become “the hand of retribution for my entire family,” The New York Times reported.
A judge had issued a temporary restraining order against Seaver as part of the proceedings, which were voluntarily dismissed Thursday in a Nashville court, multiple US media said.
Parton rose from grinding poverty to become a rhinestone-studded legend with hits like Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

She also starred in multiple films and donated millions of dollars to charities as she built a vast business empire that includes her popular Dollywood theme park in Tennessee, cosmetics, pet apparel, baking mixes and even a truck stop. — AFP

b1adb1e37c6f1d2f: JAKARTA: The Australian government has deployed a military transport aircraft to help Indonesia put out wildfires in Borneo that are causing toxic haze across the region, both countries have said.
The months-long blazes have engulfed huge tracts of land and produced air pollution that has harmed human health, drifted across borders and frayed Indonesia's ties with its neighbours.
The C-130 Hercules plane left the Indonesian capital Jakarta for East Kalimantan province on Thursday to join local water-bombing efforts, the Indonesian disaster agency chief said.

"Based on our monitoring and observations, as well as discussions with the Australian technical team, there are still many hotspots in the East Kalimantan region," Kristomei Sianturi said in a statement late on Thursday.
The C-130 can drop 15,000 litres of water per sortie, or just over 100,000 litres per day, according to a statement from the Australian embassy in Indonesia.
Ambassador Rod Brazier said the countries were "enduring friends" and recalled support that Indonesia sent to help battle Australia's own devastating bushfires in 2020.
Australia is also sending a Cessna Citation aircraft as a guide plane as well as 20 personnel, including pilots, flight crew and paramedics.
The air operation is scheduled to last for seven days, from 6 to 12 Nov.
Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas estimates the blazes consumed more than 1.9 million hectares of land in the first nine months of the year.
Experts say much of the destruction is linked to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices, often associated with the expansion of timber, palm oil and mining operations.
More than 400,000 people in Indonesia have been treated for acute respiratory ailments caused by the toxic haze, the health ministry said on Wednesday.
Japan also sent about 350 Self-Defense Forces members with three helicopters to help with firefighting efforts in West Kalimantan in September.
16ffcecc5fba2575: PETALING JAYA: Umno telah menjelaskan denda RM50 juta yang dikenakan terhadap bekas presidennya Najib Razak, sekali gus membolehkannya menjalani baki hukuman penjara berhubung sabitan kes rasuah di bawah tahanan rumah.
Dalam satu kenyataan, Setiausaha Agung Umno, Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki, berkata parti itu berjaya mengumpul dana mencukupi menerusi kempen sumbangan yang dilancarkan pada September lalu.
“Kami ingin mengucapkan terima kasih kepada ahli-ahli dan orang ramai atas sumbangan mereka,” katanya.

Peguam Najib, Farhan Shafee dan pegawai khasnya, Lutfi Azhar, sebelum itu dilihat menuju ke kaunter pembayaran Mahkamah Tinggi di ruang legar sebelum meneruskan perjalanan ke pejabat pendaftaran jenayah.
Farhan kemudian mengesahkan bahawa denda berkenaan telah dibayar.
“Kami masih di sini untuk menguruskan dokumen yang diperlukan,” katanya.
Perkembangan itu selepas beberapa jam Utusan Malaysia melaporkan dua individu yang mewakili Najib hadir ke mahkamah bagi menguruskan pembayaran denda berkenaan.
Bagaimanapun, isteri Najib, Rosmah Mansor, menafikan laporan itu.

Najib dipenjarakan pada Ogos 2022 selepas Mahkamah Persekutuan mengekalkan sabitannya atas kesalahan menyalahgunakan kuasa, pecah amanah jenayah dan pengubahan wang haram membabitkan dana RM42 juta milik SRC International.
Beliau dijatuhi hukuman penjara 12 tahun dan denda RM210 juta.

Pada Januari 2024, Yang di-Pertuan Agong ketika itu, Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah, mengurangkan separuh hukuman penjara Najib dan menurunkan jumlah dendanya kepada RM50 juta menerusi pengampunan diraja.
Pada September lalu, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim, memberikan Najib pengampunan bersyarat lanjut yang membolehkannya menjalani baki hukuman di bawah tahanan rumah sehingga 23 Ogos 2028.
Aturan itu tertakluk kepada pembayaran denda RM50 juta oleh Najib serta pematuhan terhadap syarat-syarat lain yang ditetapkan.

Menurut Berita Harian, polis memperketat kawalan keselamatan di sepanjang jalan masuk ke kediaman Najib di Jalan Langgak Duta, Kuala Lumpur, susulan spekulasi bahawa beliau mungkin pulang ke rumah petang ini.
Ketua Polis Sentul, Anuar Bakri Abdul Salam, berkata persiapan keselamatan dan pemantauan telah dilakukan sejak pagi tadi, walaupun polis masih belum menerima maklumat khusus berhubung perkara itu.
Anuar berkata persiapan berkenaan merupakan langkah berjaga-jaga dan polis bersedia menghadapi sebarang kemungkinan.
Polis mula memantau jalan masuk ke kediaman itu pada 10.30 pagi dengan mengadakan sekatan bagi menghalang individu yang tidak dibenarkan daripada menghampiri rumah berkenaan.
Lebih 50 pegawai dan anggota polis dikerahkan ke lokasi, bersama kereta peronda dan sebuah van bergerak.
Dua khemah turut didirikan bagi tujuan operasi dan keselamatan, manakala petugas media diarahkan berada di luar kawasan sekatan polis.
Kebanyakan pegawai kanan dari IPD Sentul turut dilihat berada di lokasi.
c2359736411071f1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — The Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) has issued a thunderstorm warning for several areas across six states and the Federal Territory of Putrajaya, expected to last until 2pm today.

The warning, issued in a statement at noon today, covers Pahang (Kuantan and Rompin), Selangor (Sepang, Kuala Langat, Klang, Petaling and Kuala Selangor), Putrajaya, and Johor (Kota Tinggi and Mersing).
In Sarawak, the affected areas are Mukah (Mukah, Dalat and Matu), Bintulu (Tatau and Bintulu), Sibu, Kapit (Song), Sri Aman (Lubok Antu) and Betong (Betong).

47d1b59a13fd4059: HANG TUAH JAYA: Former prime minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob says there is no reason for political parties to remain at loggerheads after the Melaka state election.

Speaking on the sidelines of Barisan Nasional's election campaign here today, he said he hoped more MPs would agree to the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) reached between the government and 13 opposition MPs last month.
“It’s not something new. I started it (in 2021),” the former Umno vice-president told reporters after a walkabout with BN’s candidate for the Durian Tunggal seat, Mustafa Musa.
“Everyone should cooperate if possible. We can oppose each other during the election, but after that, there is no reason to continue the hostilities.”
On Oct 29, the government signed a CSA with six Bersatu MPs led by its president, Muhyiddin Yassin, and seven independent MPs, including Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.
The CSA gives opposition MPs access to constituency development funds that government MPs have had access to over the past four years.

It also lists two key reforms for Putrajaya to undertake in exchange for their support - limiting the prime minister’s tenure, and separating the roles of the attorney-general and public prosecutor before the end of the parliamentary term.
Asked whether the CSA’s contents should be made public, Ismail said the government could disclose the agreement if it wanted the public to scrutinise its contents.
Perikatan Nasional chief whip Takiyuddin Hassan yesterday called on the government to make the CSA’s contents public, particularly details on allocations, disbursement mechanisms and implementation.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim yesterday said the government is prepared to reveal the contents of the CSA.
He said deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof, who oversaw the signing of the CSA, would raise the matter at today’s Cabinet meeting.

556272248e89a6db: Despite its official name “Memorandum of Understanding for Transformation and Political Stability”, it was in pith and substance a confidence and supply agreement (CSA) between the government led by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Ismail Sabri Yaakob and the main opposition Pakatan Harapan (PH) bloc led by Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
The first of its kind agreement in the country, signed on September 13, 2021, was to “cool political temperatures and allow sharper focus to fight the Covid-19 pandemic and economic malaise”.
The agreement can be read here: https://www.parlimen.gov.my/images/webuser/bkk/mou.pdf
A general view of the Parliament building in Kuala Lumpur November 6, 2025. — Picture by Yusof Isa

It was mutually agreed that the government would not propose the dissolution of Parliament before July 31, 2022, and that the government would do its best to fulfil each transformation proposal within the timeframe agreed by both sides.

PH would reciprocate by agreeing (a) to support or abstain in Parliament in the vote on Budget 2022 (to be unveiled on October 29, 2021), after mutual agreement on its content, and (b) to support or abstain in any government proposal or Bill, where failure for it to pass would be seen as a form of no-confidence vote on the government. The proposal or Bill would first have to be agreed by the government and PH.
Both sides agreed that the agreement would not prevent PH from playing its check-and-balance role.
Other than that, the government agreed to undertake to take a number of steps, one of which is parliamentary reform, involving:
tabling and approving a Parliament Service Bill to ensure Parliament as an independent institution;
equal allocations for government and opposition MPs;
membership of PSC to be more balanced;
Parliament’s Standing Orders to be amended to ensure proceedings in the Dewan rakyat and Dewan Negara would be more organised and effective; and
office of the Opposition Leader to be given appropriate rights and facilities.
So, there must be equal allocations for government and opposition MPs, which must be carried out immediately, as was the case with other steps.
As such, can it be said that the agreement, in pith and substance a CSA, was Dajjal-like?

27b05ba3be899d5e: WASHINGTON: A public commission greenlit US President Donald Trump's massive triumphal arch despite hearing hours of testimony on Thursday from dozens of furious opponents who questioned its legality and purpose.

Chief among the complaints was the location of the 250-foot (76-meter) tall structure: adjacent to the hallowed Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of American service members.
The giant arch would be much taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, its inspiration. It would also tower over the Lincoln Memorial, directly across the Potomac River.
The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to approve the project late Thursday.

The four dissenting commissioners also unsuccessfully called for the decision to be delayed, noting there were legal concerns, a lack of congressional appropriation to fund the project, and questions about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's claims of the arch's military use.
But the majority on the panel, which is controlled by Trump allies, voted against delay after one commissioner noted "the project proponent is looking for a decision tonight."
The Trump administration has said it aims to start work right away with the commission's approval, pending any last-minute court intervention.
The arch is one of several projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital, many of which have prompted legal challenges.

They include a White House ballroom, for which Trump had an entire wing of the presidential mansion demolished. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the plaintiff who filed suit to halt the project did not have standing.
Another is the repeated renovation of the Reflecting Pool, a massive rectangular water basin on the National Mall.
Trump has also proposed revamping the East Potomac Golf Links, a historic waterfront Washington golf course, cutting down hundreds of trees before a judge halted the project.

Several veterans have sued seeking to halt construction of the arch, claiming it legally requires congressional approval. The attorneys general of Washington and Virginia similarly filed suit this week against the project.
The location, a traffic circle currently covered in grass, is key to the Trump administration's defence of the project.

Proponents claim that Congress approved the construction of a monument at the site over a century ago. However, that plan envisioned two large columns, meant to signify the North and the South in the US Civil War, not an arch.
District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is overseeing the case, has ordered the Trump administration to provide notice before any work takes place at the site, which lies on the edge of the US capital.
More than 100 people, often speaking as representatives of organizations, spoke late into the evening to express their nearly unanimous opposition.
Kicking off the remarks was congressman Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which oversees public parks.
"This arch would dishonour America, our ideals, and our laws," he said, warning that contractors who work on the project could possibly be running afoul of the law.
"I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it," he said.

"Because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," he added, referring to the Democrats' winning control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.
892b5fed099e7baa: JAKARTA: Indonesian police have named a fourth senior officer as a suspect in the alleged wiretapping of President Prabowo Subianto, as authorities continue to investigate the motives behind a scandal that has exposed a deepening rift between the president and his predecessor, Joko Widodo.
The case has piled more pressure on Prabowo, with public discontent growing over his costly populist policies and weakening investor confidence in Indonesia's US$1.5 trillion economy.

At a press conference late on Thursday, police named a senior law enforcement official with the initials SU as the new suspect, and said he served as monitoring chief at Indonesia's Criminal Investigation Agency between 2010 and 2019. Local media later identified him as Slamet Uliandi.

Investigators alleged that SU, who was the head of the investigation agency's information and technology unitfrom 2021 to 2026, gave the go-ahead for the wiretapping, said cyber crime unit director Suhermanto at the press conference.

"When the other two suspects were about to wiretap, they got approval from SU. They also asked his approval before deleting interception records," Suhermanto said, adding that SU had not yet been detained due to a health condition.

Three senior police officers had already been arrested on Tuesday, including the former national police chief and Prabowo's chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is widely known as a Widodo loyalist.
Police are still investigating the motives behind the attempts to intercept Prabowo's communications, and have so far questioned 13 police officers and five criminal and IT experts.
The national police chief has also formed a special team to investigate the case, spokesman Trunoyudo Wisnu Andiko said.

Jakarta remained calm on Thursday and Friday despite the deployment of thousands of troops in the wake of the wiretapping revelations. Military tents and buses were seen in the capital, as well as a small number of soldiers.
Lawmakers are also considering a probe into the eligibility of vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Widoko's son, in what could be the first step toward removing him from office.
967fdf5012408eff: KUALA LUMPUR: Umno has settled the RM50 million fine imposed on its former president Najib Razak, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence for his graft conviction under house arrest.
In a statement, Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the party managed to collect enough funds through its donation drive, launched in September.
"We would like to thank members and the public for their contributions," he added.
Najib's lawyer Farhan Shafee and special officer Lutfi Azhar were earlier seen approaching the High Court payment counter at the lobby before proceeding to the criminal registry office.
Farhan later confirmed that the fine had been paid. "We are still here sorting out the necessary documents," he said.
Lutfi meanwhile said they were waiting for the release order.
This comes hours after Utusan Malaysia reported that two individuals representing Najib were at the court to facilitate payment of the fine.
Najib’s wife, Rosmah Mansor, however dismissed the report.
Najib was jailed in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million in SRC International funds.
He was sentenced to 12 years' jail and fined RM210 million.
In January 2024, then Yang di-Pertuan Agong Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah halved Najib’s prison sentence and reduced his fine to RM50 million as part of a royal pardon.

In September this year, the current Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.
The arrangement was subject to Najib paying the RM50 million fine and complying with other stipulated conditions.
FMT has reached out to home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, Kajang prison and the prisons department's spokesmen for comment.
According to Berita Harian, police have tightened security along the access road to Najib’s residence in Jalan Langgak Duta in Kuala Lumpur amid speculation that he could return home this afternoon.
Sentul police chief Anuar Bakri Abdul Salam said security and surveillance preparations had been in place since this morning, although police had yet to receive specific information about the matter.
Anuar said the preparations were precautionary and police were ready for any eventuality.
Police began monitoring the access road at 10.30am, setting up cordons to prevent unauthorised people from approaching the residence.
More than 50 police officers and personnel were deployed, alongside patrol cars and a mobile van.
Two tents were also set up for operational and security purposes, while media personnel were instructed to remain outside the police cordon.
Most of the senior officers from the Sentul police headquarters were also seen at the location.
a3f2d788d803aa52: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — A member of Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s legal team arrived at the Kuala Lumpur Court Complex in Jalan Duta today at noon, according to a New Straits Times report.

f0f39f0439308e62: TOKYO: Japanese tech investment giant SoftBank said Friday that China had blocked its US$5.4 billion acquisition of a Swiss-Swedish industrial robot maker.
The deal to buy ABB Robotics, announced last year, had been touted by SoftBank as part of its push into the fast-growing field of AI-powered robots.
ABB Robotics specialises in industrial machines, such as large robotic arms that can make precise movements in factories.
Its parent company ABB Group says China is its second-largest market, with more than 90% of sales there from locally made products and services.
But Beijing -- which is locked in a diplomatic spat with Japan -- has been tightening control over AI and other sensitive technologies.
SoftBank said it had received notice from Chinese regulators on Wednesday "that it had prohibited the acquisition of ABB's robotics business in China".
It said SoftBank and ABB were "working constructively on the transaction".
ABB said Thursday that SoftBank had informed it of the regulatory block.
When the acquisition was announced in October 2025, SoftBank -- a major investor in ChatGPT-creator OpenAI -- called it part of its AI-focused business strategy.
It is not the only AI-related deal barred by the Chinese government in recent months.
In April, Beijing blocked the acquisition of startup Manus, an agent tool that can carry out real-world tasks, by Facebook owner Meta after a regulatory review.
Analysts said at the time that the move was a sign of China's growing oversight of its AI sector -- a sensitive field given fierce competition with the US.
Buzz is growing around China as advanced robotics emerges as the next frontier of the AI boom, fuelling investor enthusiasm and alarm from rivals including the US.
Robots are popping up more in everyday life in China, with trial jobs including directing traffic, cleaning houses or working on factory floors.
ABB Robotics has a workforce of around 7,000, and its 2024 revenues of US$2.3 billion represented around seven percent of ABB Group's total income.
ABB Group had previously planned to spin off the robotics business as a separately listed company.
583ea33e74009fbb: Nation-state actors and criminals likely exploited the PHP2SHELL vulnerability before its disclosure, according to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince.

“These vulnerabilities, like the PHP vulnerabilities that were disclosed the other day, had been in the wild for years,” Prince said on the company’s third quarter earnings call. “We're going back through our logs looking for any evidence that hackers or nation-state actors or others had been using them in the past. I know that we're going to find examples of that.”
That was just one of the warnings he offered on the call, among them that some of Cloudflare’s customers believe AI agents are “a bane to their business and want to keep them away.”
To explain why, Prince hypothesized that he could use an agent to find him a restaurant to eat at after he finishes his day of investor relations duties.

“It might go and scour the internet and look at 1,000 different restaurants' websites, pull down 1,000 different menus, and then I might choose to only go to one of those,” he said. “The problem is that 999 of those restaurants have now had a cost that is just been applied to them, but they are not getting any benefit.”

The CEO admitted that web searches have always driven some low-value traffic but feels the volume of agentic activity – which Cloudflare has previously predicted will be one thousand times greater than clicks from humans – means the problem is now at a different scale.
Prince also had bad news for Kubernetes aficionados, because he thinks containers might become another casualty of the agentic age.

The CEO allowed that containers are “a significant improvement over bare metal or even virtual machines,” and said they fueled the growth of hyperscale clouds and mobile applications. But he thinks containers are already cooked.

“The container-based architecture of the hyperscalers and neoclouds just can't keep up in a cost-effective way with the new agentic paradigms of today,” he argued, again citing the 1000:1 ratio of bot:human traffic Cloudflare expects to see online any year now.

That’s a Cloudflare-centric view, because Prince pitched the company’s serverless “Workers” service as an alternative to containers. The company also offers products that can either block agents, ameliorate the cost and traffic impacts of agentic activity, or allow organizations to monetize traffic generated by AI.

Prince said demand for those products is growing fast, claiming that since July 1st, “approximately five percent” of the web opted in to Cloudflare’s content protection products. The CEO said Meta is already a customer, and said Zuck’s new “Muse” agents will benefit Cloudflare by creating more agentic traffic that third parties want to tame.
He also pointed to year-on-year revenue growth of 39 percent, which saw quarterly revenue reach a record $782.5 million.
And he thinks there are better days ahead, due to the terrible state of security.

“It may seem like the sky is falling with the number of new security vulnerabilities that have been reported over the last few weeks,” Prince said. “I wish I could tell you we were through the worst, but we're not.”

He thinks Cloudflare can profit from security misery because the extent of its activities and client base mean it is “among the first to receive quiet disclosure of new vulnerabilities” and remediates them before disclosure.

Investors thought this all made sense, and in after-hours trading sent Cloudflare shares up by around 15 percent, meaning it recovered and then improved on losses that it incurred earlier after major US indices dropped around four percent as investors who worry tech stocks are overvalued. ®
380e2f5c00205030: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — A year-end settlement between Sarawak and Petronas is not possible despite Sarawak Premier Tan Sri Abang Johari Openg expressing confidence that a deal could be reached before the end of the year, a political analyst said.

University of Tasmania’s James Chin said that, based on his knowledge and interactions in Sarawak, such an outcome was unlikely at present because the two sides remained fundamentally different in their interests, which is why they approached the Federal Court to resolve the deadlock in the first place.
“In that interview, although he mentioned that a deal is due by year-end, it is not possible to have the deal because court proceedings are ongoing.
“You cannot get an agreement while these court cases are happening unless Petronas withdraws, or both sides go to the courts and say they want to settle out of court,” Chin said.
Abang Johari told The Edge this week that the Petronas-Petros dispute was in its “last mile” and could be settled before the end of the year.

These negotiations come after two legal developments. Petronas filed its petition in January seeking clarity over the state and federal laws governing its operations in Sarawak. Sarawak then filed its own petition challenging the continued validity and application of several federal petroleum laws to the state.
The Federal Court has fixed Jan 25 to 29 next year to hear the two petitions, which are being kept separate and will be heard in the order in which they were filed.
The year-end target floated by the Sarawak premier also follows several earlier indications that an agreement was close.

In December last year, Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof said commercial negotiations were progressing well and that an outcome was expected in early 2026. He had earlier said only administrative and commercial issues remained unresolved.

By June this year, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said several important issues had been ironed out and a final agreement was expected soon, although analysts later cautioned that the continuing court cases showed that key legal and commercial questions remained unresolved.
Analysts say credibility in a deal could be undermined by continued promises without resolution.

“Missing the year-end target could raise questions about GPS’s credibility, particularly since Sarawak’s government had previously anticipated a commercial agreement by December 2025,” analyst Jamil Ghani said.
“Repeated assurances without tangible outcomes could gradually undermine confidence in the process.”
Universiti Malaya’s Azman Awang Pawi agreed that the deadline had created a benchmark against which the state government’s negotiating effectiveness could be judged.

“If the deadline passes without an agreement, opposition parties could question why a government with such a strong political mandate and considerable influence at the federal level has yet to secure a definitive settlement,” he said.
However, Azman cautioned against treating a missed deadline as a serious political setback in itself.

He said the dispute involved complex constitutional, regulatory and commercial questions which could not necessarily be resolved according to an electoral timetable, with the continuing legal proceedings themselves showing that important jurisdictional questions remained unsettled.
Azman said GPS also entered the election with considerable political capital built up through its wider autonomy agenda, development programmes and stable control of the state government.
A delayed agreement alone was therefore unlikely to seriously weaken the coalition.
“The greater risk emerges if negotiations repeatedly produce optimistic announcements without concrete implementation.”

Azman said Abang Johari’s standing would ultimately depend less on whether an agreement was signed by Dec 31 than on whether Sarawakians believed meaningful progress had been made without compromising the state’s long-term interests.

“If a final agreement is delayed but both sides can demonstrate clear consensus on regulatory responsibilities, commercial arrangements, Petros’s operational role and future revenue opportunities, the political damage may be limited,” he said.
Azman added that Sarawak’s petroleum aspirations and Petronas’s national mandate need not be mutually exclusive.

“The strongest outcome would be an agreement that converts constitutional disagreement into institutional cooperation, commercial certainty and greater economic benefits for Sarawak and Malaysia,” he said.
“That would be a stronger legacy for Abang Johari and GPS than any short-term electoral advantage gained from confrontation.”
6975dd1c12be3208: HONG KONG, Nov 6 — Asian tech firms suffered a bloodbath today as investors tracked a collapse on Wall Street fuelled by fears that Democrats will ramp up regulations of the AI industry following their blowout victory in this week’s US midterm elections.

Trading boards were a sea of red in early business, with Seoul and Tokyo taking the brunt of the selling as traders fled to the hills amid uncertainty about a sector that had pushed stock markets to record highs just five months ago.

While the historic “blue wave” in Tuesday’s vote had been initially welcomed on hopes it could put pressure on President Donald Trump to wind down his war against Iran, fears about the impact on the AI buildout soon came to the fore.
Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.
Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.

The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.
The eye-watering rally in many companies’ valuations had also caused unease on trading floors.

Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights said investors were selling up because of “concerns that we might see greater opposition to AI buildout plans, with the results in Texas prompting concerns that politicians in the state might target Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX due to his support for Trump”.

New York’s Nasdaq plunged 5.5 per cent in its worst day—perentage-wise—since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. The S&P 500 tanked more than four percent and the Dow more than three percent.
Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16 per cent this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.

Trump blamed the collapse on the Democrats, writing on Truth Social: “The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday - So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
The heavy selling continued in Asia.
Seoul plunged almost nine per cent at one point, with chip giant SK hynix off 10 per cent while rival Samsung was eight per cent down.
The Kospi more than doubled between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, and has since then lost almost 50 per cent.
Tokyo dived seven per cent as Kioxia and SoftBank gave back more than 10 per cent, with Advantest more than eight percent lower.
TSMC’s seven-per cent drop dragged Taipei’s Taiex around eight per cent lower.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney and Singapore were all down more than one per cent, with Wellington and Manila also in the red.
“The blood is in the streets, folks,” said Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets.

“The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre buildout... this looks totally overdone but the nature of sell-everything of this market means we need to look for some stability first.”
The mood was also dampened by a fresh lift in oil prices, extending Thursday’s gains after plunging on the midterm results amid hopes for an end to the Iran war.
Traders were keeping eyes on developments in the crisis after US and Iranian leaders had indicated progress earlier in the week.
US jobs data is also due later in the day, following broadly positive readings earlier in the week. — AFP
d690f567e6743ac1: PARIS, Nov 6 — Fans of the violent Grand Theft Auto video game franchise are just two weeks away from getting their hands on the latest edition, which has taken almost a decade to make and has become the most expensive title in history.

The franchise allows players to act out gangster fantasies — shooting up bars, crashing cars — in fictional renderings of US cities where the soundtrack piped through in-game radio is almost as important as the cutting-edge visuals.

GTA VI, which comes 13 years after its predecessor, is expected to break sales records when it lands on November 19 thanks in part to a monumental marketing campaign that kicked off in late 2023 with the first official trailer.
“It is going to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time,” Chris Dring of The Game Business outlet told AFP.
The previous edition, GTA V, is still the second-biggest selling game ever — it took just three days to rack up $1 billion in sales, two days less than the movie Avengers: Endgame.

The budget of GTA VI has reportedly ballooned to over $1 billion — far higher than any other game or film — and projections have it on track to make several billion in its first week, which would smash all records for any cultural product.
‘Top creators’
GTA VI has two main protagonists, former drug-runner Jason and newly released ex-con Lucia, who try to survive in Vice City, a reimagining of Miami.
Lucia is the first playable woman character in a main edition of the almost 30-year history of a franchise.
During the 1990s and 2000s the game’s graphic depictions of sex, violence and misogyny became notorious — tabloid media outrage boosting the title’s notoriety and helping sales to skyrocket.
Rockstar Games has spent eight years developing the sixth edition, a process beset by difficulties including the leak of development footage and code for the game online in 2022.
But expectations are sky-high.
“They’ve spent a long time on this game, but they are probably the top game entertainment creators in the world,” said Dring.
Analysts expect the game to have an impact on the entire video game sector, including on console sales and accessories.
Several other studios delayed the release of new games to avoid being caught in the hype cycle around GTA VI.
Analysis firm Sensor Tower said the game had already generated around $750 million from pre-sales.
Surveys suggested almost one-third of the 49 million people who use PS5 and Xbox Series consoles in the United States intended to buy the game.
“The purchase intent that we’re seeing on ‘Grand Theft Auto’ is far away above any other game we’ve ever tracked,” said Mat Piscatella of consultancy Circana.
“For me, it’s the game of the decade,” Jocelin Lebeau, 39, a gamer who works for the French military, told AFP at a recent event in Paris.
“I’m ready to buy it sight unseen.” — AFP
f3b4e01969bd532e: BEIJING: The midterm drubbing of Donald Trump's Republicans may strengthen China's hand in trade talks with Washington, but Beijing is unlikely to revel in the misfortunes of a US president whose successor could prove less accommodating.
US voters angered by rising living costs, exacerbated by Trump's trade wars with China and other countries, turned on his party in Tuesday's vote, handing Democrats control of Congress.

That political humbling should make Trump more wary of unsettling a fragile trade truce with Beijing, some political analysts said, giving China a potential advantage in negotiations set to resume later this month.

Washington's divided political landscape also gives Beijing space to fortify itself and diversify its trade ties before a potentially less China-friendly US administration takes power, some Chinese and Western analysts added.
"The Chinese are very realistic that a new president might be very different (from Trump)," said Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese Foreign Ministry ​official.

"But if we can have two more years of stability, that's already a good thing for China ... The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war," added Shen, who now works for Beijing-based think tank Global Governance Institution.
The next two years, however, may not be smooth sailing for Beijing, other analysts said.

The risk is that Trump, constrained at home, becomes more aggressive in seeking foreign policy wins, while a Democratic-controlled Congress may push him harder to unfreeze arms sales to Taiwan, a red line for Beijing.
"There are more foreign policy actions that Trump can take that are unconventional and untold,” said senior China analyst Chim Lee at the Economist Intelligence Unit.

"The broad direction of US-China policy isn't necessarily going to change, but I think that the concern is around less conventional foreign policy issues that would have unexpected ramifications for China,” he said.

Top among the concerns is an escalation of the Iran war into a wider regional conflict. That could trigger a sustained spike in global oil prices, threaten China's energy security and disrupt Beijing’s ties in the Middle East.

In the short term, attention turns to imminent trade talks, with Trump set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month and then in Miami in December for the G20.
At stake is a truce in a trade war - expiring in January - that averted a major shock to the global economy last year.

Beijing could conclude that Trump's political problems mean he needs a deal more than China, encouraging Chinese negotiators to press harder for tariff reductions and other US concessions, said Craig Singleton, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a US think tank.
However, that also risks a "miscalculation that unsettles the very stability Xi is trying to preserve," he added.

Trump has repeatedly railed against what he sees as China's unfair trade with Washington, slapping triple-digit tariffs on Chinese goods shortly after he returned to office last year to address a trade imbalance he said was "killing" the United States.
However, he has since significantly softened his tone, feting Xi at two grand summits in Beijing and Washington that delivered few tangible economic wins.

Trump's bonhomie with Xi stands in contrast to his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, who repeatedly angered China with comments over human rights issues and a pledge that the US would defend Taiwan if Beijing attacked. Some of Trump's potential Republican successors, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are also seen by analysts as more hawkish on China.

After the midterms, Trump could be even less willing to upset the stable relationship he has developed with China, said Wu Xinbo, a professor at Shanghai's Fudan University who advises China's Foreign Ministry.

Beyond trade, Trump may also seek to enlist Beijing's help to secure other foreign policy wins as the clock ticks on his presidency – such as ending the war between Russia and Ukraine or arranging another summit with North Korea's Kim Jong Un.
Beijing, which maintains deep trade ties with Russia and North Korea, could use that leverage in exchange for concessions from Trump, analysts said.

But after years of dealing primarily with Trump, Beijing now faces a Congress far more intent on pressing human rights issues, scrutinizing Chinese investments and delivering a US$14 billion package of arms to Taiwan that Trump has said he is withholding as a "negotiating chip" with Xi.
China claims democratically governed Taiwan and has asked for the arms sales to stop.
"The Chinese will definitely react strongly against that," said Shen, the former Chinese Foreign Ministry ​official, calling it "risk number one" after the midterms.

a85ec66a1a867064: TOKYO: Tokyo said Friday it had demanded the immediate release of Japan Tobacco's assets seized in Russia, as relations with Moscow sour following the arrest of a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.
The seizure, which the Kremlin ordered Thursday, is the latest move against a foreign company's Russian operations under rules that Moscow casts as retribution for international sanctions.
Japan Tobacco is one of the world's biggest tobacco companies and holds around 40% of the Russian cigarette market, according to media reports.

Japanese government spokesman Minoru Kihara said that two senior officials from Tokyo visiting Russia "had lodged a protest with the Russian government together with the ambassador of Japan to Russia, and demanded the immediate withdrawal of the measure".
Japan Tobacco said Friday that four of the group's manufacturing subsidiaries had been placed under temporary control and it was assessing "possible actions".
"Our group has continued its business operations in Russia while complying with all domestic and international sanctions and regulations," the firm said in a statement.
A decree issued by President Vladimir Putin on Thursday said the assets would be taken into "temporary administration".
Control of the company's Russian operations has been handed to a Russian company called "Industrial Assets", the decree stipulated.
Ryosei Akazawa, Japan's minister for economy, trade and industry, said Friday that Tokyo had been "on alert" to the risk to Japanese interests in Russia.
The officials who had lodged the protest had been on a business trip at the time of the seizure to push for the safeguard of Japanese companies' assets, he added.
Several European firms have seen their Russian operations effectively lost -- most recently Swiss food conglomerate Nestle and French supermarket giant Auchan.
Hundreds of foreign companies left Russia in the wake of its full-scale invasion in Ukraine in February 2022, but many others chose to stay.
Moscow slapped tough financial restrictions on companies from so-called "unfriendly" countries that have put sanctions on Moscow over the war.
Japan, which has a decades-old dispute with Moscow over a string of islands in the Pacific, has joined in some sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Russia's FSB security service arrested Japanese journalist Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper last month on allegations of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory".
The foreign ministry in Moscow has also accused Tokyo of systematically using journalists for espionage operations inside the country.
