e8800235b886483c: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 6 — Silicon Valley bosses who spent two years cozying up to US President Donald Trump now face a Democratic Congress already threatening subpoenas, after midterm elections in which antipathy toward artificial intelligence swayed voters.
“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said on Tuesday.
Senator Ed Markey, for his part, warned tech executives they would need to “plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

It is a cold shower for tech bosses who rallied behind Trump after his 2024 win, with Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and others front and center at his January 2025 inauguration.

Musk went furthest, spending more than US$250 million to help elect Trump and then taking charge of his DOGE cost-cutting drive. He poured nearly half a billion dollars more into backing Republicans in the midterms.
Once they take control of both chambers on January 3, Democrats will control the committees that can compel an executive to testify or hand over internal documents under threat of prosecution.
In 2020, the heads of Amazon, Apple, Facebook and Google were called to answer for their market dominance.
Musk, OpenAI’s Sam Altman or Nvidia’s Jensen Huang—one of Trump’s closest advisers on AI—could now face the same ordeal.
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, elected senator for Michigan despite more than US$5 million spent against him by America PAC, the political committee funded by Musk, wants to go further.
He is calling for a “full-on pause” in the development of the most powerful AI systems and a US-China treaty to “pause and ban superintelligence,” meaning AI that would surpass human intelligence.
To pass legislation, however, lawmakers will need to rally a party divided on the issue and overcome the veto of Trump, who remains president until January 2029.
No major tech boss had commented on the election as of yesterday except Musk, who joked: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
Parts of the industry had begun distancing themselves from Republicans before the vote.

The main pro-AI political fund, financed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz—one of whose cofounders backed Trump in 2024 — received no new donations from April through the end of September, as public distrust of AI grew.
Meta has hired former Democratic staffers in recent months to represent it in Congress, according to Axios.
Shapeshifters
Criticism is also coming from the Republican side.
“Voters are primed to reward whichever political party delivers on holding Big Tech accountable,” Daniel Cochrane, a senior fellow at the conservative Institute for Family Studies, told AFP.
“In this election, concerns about AI’s social and economic impacts shifted votes,” he said, pointing to data centers as well as AI’s effects on jobs and children.
According to an NBC News exit poll, AI and data centers were “a crucial or a major factor” for 56 percent of voters in their choice for Congress.
“Let’s not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate,” said Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, an influential centrist coalition funded by major tech companies.

“There’s only one thing that sinks the US economy, it’s the AI trade,” and “the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers,” Chamath Palihapitiya warned during an election-night livestream of the All-In podcast, which he co-hosts with other prominent pro-Trump Silicon Valley investors.
Even market analyst Dan Ives, known for his bullish outlook on tech growth, now estimates that 10 percent of the 800 to 1,000 new data centers planned in the United States “will not happen.”
“The tech bros are shapeshifters,” said Cochrane, who expects Zuckerberg “to have another mea culpa” before an “aggressive Dem congress.”
“Ultimately, the tech bros are for the tech bros,” he said. — AFP
bcfb9bcac42e4fc4: SHANGHAI: The dollar held steady against major currencies on Friday, after a sharp selloff in US equities drove investors toward haven assets such as the yen and pushed Treasury yields lower ahead of a closely watched government payrolls report.
The trigger for the retreat from risk was a Democratic sweep in Congress that hammered US stocks on Thursday, with the Nasdaq recording its deepest one-day drop since "Liberation Day" in April 2025.
Fears of tighter scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry, particularly around data centre construction, has roiled global markets this week.
The equity rout prompted investors to find shelter in bonds and haven currencies. The yen strengthened 0.2% to a one-week high of 157.40 a US dollar before reversing some of that gain.
The Swiss franc firmed 0.2% against the US currency. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against six peers, was roughly flat at 101.55.

"The AI selloff is creating competing forces for the dollar," OCBC analysts said. "Falling US yields are blunting the dollar's safe-haven appeal, leaving the yen as the standout hedge against more US-centric volatility, while flows from Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund could provide another tailwind for the yen."
The flight to safety drove the 10-year Treasury yield down overnight. It was last trading at 4.84% in the Asian morning, near its lowest level since Sept 10.
The two-year yield, which is more sensitive to interest rate expectations, fell about 10 basis points overnight to 4.47%.

The move in bonds also reflected a repricing of Federal Reserve expectations, with fed funds futures scaling back the probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike in December to around 70% from more than 80% on Wednesday, traders said.
The euro was flat against the dollar at US$1.1222, but poised for a 0.5% rise for the week, ending two weeks of loss.

Next on the agenda is Friday's US non-farm payrolls report from which investors will try and gauge the Federal Reserve's rate path. Data on Thursday offered an upbeat prelude, with weekly initial jobless claims falling by 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 — matching a 57-year low in July and below the 196,000 estimate in a Reuters poll of economists.
"Recent data suggests improvement in the labour market, and we expect that to continue with this report," MUFG analysts said, referring to the non-farm payrolls data.

"Treasuries have just had a sizeable decline in rates heading into Friday's release. While we could see some of that move reverse, as long as we remain in a downward channel in rates, we recommend buying any meaningful dip on a stronger-than-expected number."
The sterling was last up 0.1% at US$1.3457 after the Bank of England raised its policy interest rate as widely expected.
16ade08f04c7d18d: Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana. A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.

Faktoje is a certified signatory of the Code of Principles of the International Fact-Finding Network and the Code of Standards of the European Fact-Checking Standards Network. Both require high levels of public transparency in disclosing sources of funding and methodologies of work. This coordinated campaign aims to undermine the impact of Faktoje’s important work by maliciously using financial information that the organization voluntarily publishes, but stripping it of context and mischaracterizing its influence.

Faktoje considers these attacks to be directly connected to its fact-checking activities under its partnership with Meta, in the context of its recent fact-checking work covering the ongoing protests and debunking misleading narratives targeting protesters.

Since its inception eight years ago, Faktoje has stood at the forefront of the fight for freedom of expression, independent journalism, and information integrity in Albania and the wider Balkans region, including participation in the regional Western Balkans Anti-Disinformation Hub, the Anti-Disinformation Network for the Balkans and the continent-wide European Digital Media Observatory – EDMO Network.

Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community. Albanian authorities and European institutions need to speak up publicly for independent fact-checkers and journalists, and to ensure their safety, while media outlets reporting on civil society funding need to do so accurately and in context.

Global Voices joins the European Fact-Checking Standards Network and the International Fact-Checking Network in vehemently condemning those attacks on our partner. We stand in solidarity with our colleagues.

4e7f81c4ff53615b: It appears that the dust has settled, at least for now as the judicial process takes over, on the Tabung Haji (TH) “mismanagement” issue.
It was widely commented upon following the release of the full royal commission of inquiry (RCI) report just before a state election.
There were allegations of embezzlement (sakau) and unadulterated corruption at this investment institution.
Presumably the intention was to throw dirt on the past administration.
Mind you the full RCI report had been on the back burner for almost three years before its release.

Some say, tactically speaking as in urban guerrilla political warfare, it was kept under wraps for an opportune time such that its release could inflict the highest degree of damage to the political opposition.
Sadly, that was not to be as the state election results stand testimony.
To add a degree of altruistic intent, the reason offered was that it could not be released earlier as the flagship, TH, was being given time to keep its policies and practices in order.

It was vehemently argued that releasing the RCI findings earlier might have affected TH’s credibility as an institution set up specifically to enable investors to finance their trips to the holy land (through consistent savings).

Worse still, it was rationalised that its depositors, largely from the country’s heartland, may have withdrawn their deposits en masse. This desperate action would have resulted in financial chaos with spillover effects on other financial institutions in the country.
To the naïve, uninformed and politically ignorant, this justification had a degree of credence.

A lawmaker had highlighted possible offences (crimes which include financial deception, falsification of accounting records, the unlawful distribution of ‘hibah’ dividends), as the Tabung Haji Act 1995 forbids declaring or paying profits when liabilities exceed assets.

To top it off, as a safe measure, criminal breach of trust is included. That is indeed a mouthful but then politicians are known for rhetoric, most times self-serving, and in certain instances illogical.

To date two ex-ministers have been charged. At the crux is the Attorney-General’s Chambers’s decision to charge the ex-CEO and ex-chief financial officer with “misleading the board” under Section 417 of the Penal Code.
The legal system only looks at the charge and decides on guilt or innocence. The reasons for such a criminal act, altruistic or not, are inconsequential.

In TH’s case it is common knowledge that the beneficiaries of this “misleading” were the investors who were paid handsome dividends. This state of affairs should not have been so as the provisions of an Act were breached.

It is obvious that the persons involved at TH accrued no gains. It is neither embezzlement nor corruption — if so, the charges would be completely different and fall under the MACC Act 2009 or Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001.
Nonetheless, this episode was milked for what it is worth to cast aspersions reflecting on the integrity and level of corruption of the government of the day.

The inquiry examined TH’s management and operations between 2014 and 2020. It concluded that the combination of high hibah commitments, governance weaknesses and accounting shortcomings affected its long-term financial sustainability.

For context, the RCI found that pressure to maintain high hibah payouts contributed to the deterioration of the fund’s financial position and pushed it towards riskier investment decisions. Unfortunately, these led to certain investments turning sour.

In its report, the RCI said LTH continued declaring attractive hibah between 2014 and 2017 despite its weakening financial position, presumably increasing pressure on management to generate higher returns.
“The attractive returns encouraged more deposits from savers, increasing TH’s financial obligations while creating expectations that similar levels of hibah would continue”.

It is obvious here who benefitted from the higher returns – the investors. Surely there is a moral justification here as the interests of the investors was paramount – Where is the “sakau”, or embezzlement as alleged by certain quarters.
How it was done, through revaluations of assets or flouting global accounting standards and whether or not there was criminal intent, is left for the courts to decide.
This expectation on higher investment returns cannot be denied. An element of greed entered the equation and no one questioned it, notwithstanding the audited accounts.
By law, no crime can be justified by the circumstances leading to it or supporting it within the ecosystem.

In an unrelated incident to provide perspective, on Nov 2, a 43-year-old unemployed father of five was sentenced to six months’ jail for stealing RM394 worth of baby formula and groceries from a supermarket in Kelantan.
It was commented that an accused’s financial hardship and family responsibilities did not automatically warrant a lighter sentence.
A proverb from the Tirukkural, an ancient Tamil literary work written by philosopher Tiruvalluvar, was quoted by the magistrate.
This only reinforces the point that the reason is inconsequential, heart breaking as it is.

In the case of TH, where is the moral ground? The investors received dividends which they were not entitled to as the Act specifically provides the stipulation on the relationship between the assets and liabilities before dividends can be declared.

In brief, investors have no good title to the dividends as it was a result of a criminal act purportedly committed by the ex-CEO and ex-CFO in misleading the board – who themselves are held to account on their fiduciary duties (healthy, professional scepticism).
This has resulted in a burden to the government in relation to the special purpose vehicle created to prevent the pilgrim fund from insolvency (circa RM10 billion).

Who will take the high road to return the dividends for the affected years. Now that TH is in a healthy state perhaps future dividends should be channelled not to the investors but to fund the special purpose vehicle.
This is food for thought in the years where “sakau” is being freely thrown about to show fellow politicians in a bad light — just to score points.
The word “sakau” has deep negative connotations. It should be used judiciously and not crowed about at any half opportunity. This action is in itself unethical
As the man fed his hungry children, does the end justify the means? Do we need to keep investors happy or is there more to it – what are their obligations?
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

7b483b246446b1a6: India’s Computer Emergency Response Team has warned the nation’s financial services industry of a “significant escalation” in attacks by what it describes as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor” that has re-targeted victims after they flubbed remediation efforts.

CERT-IN first detected the attacks in October and issued advisory in which it warned digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and wallet operators that attackers were targeting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints. If the attackers found a way in, they tried to use payment APIs to steal money.
On Thursday, the CERT published an update in which it said it continues to hear of successful attacks, including from outfits that tried to remediate their systems after earlier incidents.

“The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response,” the CERT warned.
CERT-IN has decided the attackers need a name and chose “CRAFTY FALCON.”

The security org has also revealed that the crew uses AI-enhanced tools including the ARTEX pen-testing tool, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework – all of which have been linked to users who appear to speak Chinese.

CRAFTY FALCON’s tactics see it go looking for internet-exposed environments used for testing or development, where it finds artefacts such as shared credentials, tokens, or network paths that help it move into production systems.

If it gets in, the crew re-writes victims’ applications so they do things like make unauthorized API calls. Victims’ defenses assume that only legitimate apps would call those APIs, so activity conducted by the re-written apps aren’t flagged as an attack.

Even if victims suspect an attack, they have a lot to cope with because CERT-IN says CRAFTY FALCON creates many “functionally identical variants refined in rapid succession; a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.”
The crew also quickly exploits newly discovered vulnerabilities to keep its attacks fresh.

Once it gets a toehold, the criminal crew makes tiny payments of about $0.01 to test if its attacks work. If those transfers work, CRAFTY FALCON makes larger payments. When the target is a cryptocurrency exchange or virtual digital asset service provider, the crew steals wallet keys and empties cryptocurrency wallets.

Vendors of observability tools will be warming up their Indian sales teams today, because CERT-IN’s advice to Indian businesses includes improving their ability to log events, monitor for anomalies in real time, and send alerts. It also urged keeping test environments off the internet, and restricting access to cloud resources because CRAFTY FALCON is fond of using them to run its attacks.
CERT-IN also warns that the attacks are “active and escalating” and therefore worthy of 24x7 monitoring.
Interestingly, the CERT’s advisory mentions attacks on “entities” across banking, financial services, and insurance, but only names the kind of businesses mentioned above as having reported attacks.

The Register points this out because India is home to literally thousands of banks, many of them small operations that sometimes lack basic infosec protections. CRAFTY FALCON therefore has a target-rich environment in India should it choose to expand its activities. ®
f14d060d799ecdc4: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — The ringgit opened lower against the US dollar on Friday, as mixed signals from the United States economy and financial markets weighed on the greenback’s outlook.
At 8 am, the local note eased to 4.0450/0520 against the greenback from yesterday’s close of 4.0445/0490.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the US Dollar Index (DXY) edged up 0.03 per cent to 101.60, supported by signs of resilience in the US labour market.
He said the labour market indicator, such as initial jobless claims, fell further to 189,000 last week, suggesting the US labour market remained healthy.
“Still, the two- and 10-year US Treasury yields dropped 12 and five basis points to 4.46 per cent and 4.83 per cent, respectively.
“This suggests that the markets seem unconvinced about the rate-tightening cycle and perhaps also indicates that the scope for rate hikes has gradually diminished,” he told Bernama.

Afzanizam added that the planned expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres would come under further scrutiny by the US Congress in 2027, potentially affecting optimism over valuations in the sector.

This development could weigh on optimism about the sector’s valuation. At the same time, the sharp decline in technology-related stocks suggested investors had become increasingly wary of the premium attached to the sector.
“On that note, the ringgit is likely to stay within a narrow band of RM4.04 to RM4.05 today,” he said.
The ringgit traded mostly higher against a basket of major currencies.

It appreciated against the euro to 4.5413/5492 from 4.5428/5478 at Thursday’s close, edged up vis-a-vis the British pound to 5.4421/4516 from 5.4455/4516, but fell versus the Japanese yen to 2.5683/5729 from 2.5548/5578 previously.
Meanwhile, the ringgit performed mixed against its ASEAN peers.
It gained versus the Singapore dollar to 3.1646/1706 from the previous close of 3.1679/1717, and increased against the Thai baht to 12.0836/1122 from 12.1013/1199 yesterday.
The local currency inched down versus the rupiah to 223.7/224.1 from 223.6/224.0 from Thursday’s close, and was flat vis-a-vis the Philippine peso at 6.42/6.43. — Bernama
dd79e7e62b866f76: TOKYO: Japanese and South Korean shares plunged Friday after US shares tumbled overnight on worries that midterm election results could slow or derail the artificial intelligence data center investment boom.
Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.1% to 56,930 points in early trade.
Seoul's Kospi index dived 8.5% to 4,923 -- triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes.
Investors had initially cheered Tuesday's Democratic drubbing of US President Donald Trump's Republican Party.
But they have since taken a more anxious stance, centered on worries that the electoral shakeup will hit key AI investments seen as important to economic growth.
Of the major US indices, the most impacted was the tech-focused Nasdaq, which finished down 5.5% in a sell-off that battered Nvidia and other semiconductor stocks.
It was the Nasdaq's worst session in terms of percentage loss since April 2025.
In South Korea on Friday, memory chip makers -- whose advanced chips are used alongside other data-crunching semiconductors to power AI tools -- also suffered.
Samsung Electronics plunged nearly 10% while SK hynix fell more than 11%.
The tech rout also hit chip-related shares in Japan, with Tokyo Electron shares trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

"Following the Democratic victory in the midterm elections, concerns about stricter regulations on AI-related technologies have led to a sell-off across the entire (US) market, particularly in technology stocks, causing all three major US market indices to decline," online brokerage Monex said.
"In particular, there are concerns that stricter regulations on data center construction will slow down construction projects."
Governments and tech giants worldwide are racing to build data centres to train and run AI models -- part of a global construction boom costing hundreds of billions of dollars.

d773c67d102d324d: Chris Hyde/Getty ImagesThe Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) reaches its semi-finals this weekend, in a tournament that’s been marked by upsets, nail-biting finishes and some lopsided scorelines. On Saturday in Newcastle, New Zealand’s Kiwi Ferns face Fetu Samoa in the women’s competition, before the Kiwis take on an unbeaten Tonga. Sunday’s matches in Sydney see Australia’s Jillaroos meet Fiji, while their counterparts the Kangaroos face Samoa in a rematch of the previous RLWC men’s final. Pacific nations feature in all four semi-finals. But while the teams represent countries across the region, the vast majority of their players were born in Australia or New Zealand. Our analysis of the semi-final squads found 85% of the women and 95% of the men were born in these two countries. Many have also represented other nations during their international careers. These figures speak to the tight connections between Pacific countries, Australia and New Zealand – and the opportunities rugby league offers players with ties to more than one nation. Small populations, big ties By comparing squad profiles with population data, we can see how migration, family connections and population trends are reflected on the rugby league field. Population size is no guarantee of success in international rugby league. England and France, with populations of around 59 million and 66 million respectively, have already been eliminated. Yet Tonga, home to just 105,000 people, has reached the men’s semi-finals. The Cook Islands, with fewer than 15,000 residents, is the smallest country represented at the tournament. Although the Cook Islands is not in the semi-finals, seven players across the remaining squads have previously represented this proud nation, including Kiwi stars Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad and Apii Nicholls. Generations of migration across Te Moana Nui a Kiwa (the Pacific Ocean) and the Tasman Sea have created deep family ties between these countries. In the women’s semi-finals, 57% of players were born in Australia and another 28% in New Zealand. Twelve players across the Kiwi Ferns and Samoa squads have previously represented other countries, highlighting the overlapping national ties within Pacific rugby league. The Australia-Fiji semi-final, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Only one Jillaroos player in the final team list, Tiana Penitani Gray, has previously represented another country (Tonga), while none of Fiji’s players have done so. Club affiliations show a similar concentration in Australia: 86% of players across the four women’s semi-final squads compete in the National Rugby League Women’s Premiership (NRLW). They are based mostly with Australian clubs, though seven play with New Zealand’s Warriors Women. Fiji is the only team to draw heavily on players from outside the competition. A younger Pacific In the men’s semi-finals, 95% of players were born in Australia (50%) or New Zealand (45%). Seventeen players in the NZ-Tonga squads have previously represented another country, while just two players across the four men’s semi-final teams compete outside the National Rugby League (NRL). The strong presence of NRL and NRLW players also highlights the sporting opportunities available in Australia and New Zealand, and the increasingly diverse populations of both countries. We see such trends in wider migration patterns. In 2023, Australia and New Zealand recorded net migration gains, while Tonga, Samoa and Fiji experienced net losses. Another notable demographic trend is the relatively young populations of Pacific nations. As governments around the world prepare for ageing populations and growing demand for services and pensions, the Pacific remains comparatively youthful. That’s interestingly mirrored in the World Cup squads. In the women’s competition, New Zealand (median age 27 years) and Australia (26) have considerably older squads than Fiji and Samoa (both 22). The pattern is similar among the men, with New Zealand (29) and Australia (28) fielding older squads than Samoa (26) and Tonga (24). The differences are even more pronounced in the wider populations. The median ages of New Zealanders (37) and Australians (38) are much higher than those of people in Fiji (28), Tonga (21) and Samoa (20). Within New Zealand, we can point to a similar pattern. The median age of NZ Europeans is 42, compared with 29 for Fijian New Zealanders, 24 for Samoan New Zealanders and 22 for Tongan New Zealanders. These younger populations offer what we call a “demographic dividend”: the potential economic benefits as a growing share of the population enters its working and income-earning years. But these benefits aren’t automatic. Realising them requires investment in young people’s health, education and skills, as well as opportunities to develop their talents and aspirations. When talent meets opportunity Many players representing Pacific nations in this weekend’s semi-finals grew up a long way from the islands they now represent. They and their families were drawn to Australia and New Zealand by opportunities in education, employment and sport. Yet when the chance came, many chose to wear the jersey that reflects their identity, family ties and culture. Their achievements show what’s possible when young people have opportunities to develop their talents. Building on that momentum means continuing to invest in young people, on and off the field, so the next generation can thrive – wherever they call home. f2e22fb3444c9086: From Boo Jia Cher
The federal government’s plan to build 22km of covered pedestrian walkways across Kuala Lumpur is a welcome breath of fresh air.
For a city long dominated by cars, seeing Putrajaya and Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) invest RM55 million in walking infrastructure shows an encouraging shift in mindset.
It reflects the recognition of a basic truth: people won’t walk to buses and trains if they are soaked by sudden downpours or exhausted by intense heat, so they opt for the car instead.
A roof over our heads is a strong start, but it will not magically turn Kuala Lumpur into a walkable city overnight.
The theory of walkability

American urban designer Jeff Speck popularised the “General Theory of Walkability”, which states that for people to choose walking over driving, a path must meet four conditions at the same time: it must be useful, safe, comfortable, and interesting.
A covered walkway addresses only part of one of these conditions — making the walk more comfortable by blocking out rain and sun. On its own, shelter leaves the other three major gaps untouched:

Useful: A sheltered roof is useless if the path suddenly stops at a dead end, fails to connect to a train station, or nearby homes or shops. KL’s fragmented design often leaves transit stations, housing and shops all cut off from one another.

Safe: A roof cannot protect a pedestrian from a six-lane road with fast and dangerous traffic. If there are no safe crossings, traffic lights, or bollards separating people from speeding cars, walking will seem unsafe and people will still stay in their cars.

Interesting: Streets need active shopfronts, trees, and open views to feel secure and inviting. Just looking at how crowded certain parts of KL like Petaling Street or Jalan Tuanku Abdul Rahman get, even with their flaws, shows that with lots to see while walking, people will enjoy the walk.
If DBKL simply installs roofs over disconnected or dangerous paths, the RM55 million project risks becoming performative infrastructure; a ribbon-cutting gesture rather than a genuine transformation.
Get the right people involved
To get this right, the government needs more than just a construction budget; it needs an inclusive walkability commission.
This commission should carry out thorough, ground-level walking audits across every planned route. Crucially, these audits must be inclusive.

The team cannot just sit in offices looking at blueprints. They must walk the paths alongside wheelchair users, parents pushing strollers, senior citizens, visually impaired residents, and daily transit commuters, at different times of the day.
An inclusive audit asks practical, everyday questions:
Is the curb ramp too steep for a wheelchair user?
Does the covered walkway suddenly drop off into a high-speed slip road?
Are tactile paving tiles correctly aligned for visually impaired walkers?
Is there adequate street lighting to make the route safe at night?
More than roofs over walkways
Putting a roof over KL’s streets sends an important message: that walking matters.
But if we genuinely want people to leave their cars behind and use public transport, we need more than covered walkways. We need paths that are safe, continuous and accessible to everyone.
Even a covered walkway can feel uncomfortable when the surrounding streets are dark and deserted at night, with businesses shuttered.

A lack of activity after hours can make a place feel unsafe and discourage people from walking. This is part of a much bigger conversation about walkability, one that is inseparable from how we plan and build our cities.
Let’s not just cover our walkways. Let’s fix the walk, and the city around it.
Boo Jia Cher is an FMT reader.

8424b8cbc8e88fa1: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
One connection, works every time, needs no retries

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
f87ca9d921a68dd3: Is China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries—including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods—are the envy of the world, and its tech and AI industries are second only to the US, with Europe trailing far behind.
On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time?

In a recent Brookings paper, the International Monetary Fund’s Yuanchen Yang and I explore the striking parallels between today’s China and Japan in the 1990s, especially in residential and commercial real estate as well as related infrastructure.
In both cases, the collapse of the speculative frenzy left a massive construction overhang that can take years to work off. China is still in the middle of that process.

Stunningly, China has built more square metres of residential property per capita than either the UK or France, despite still being a much poorer country. Its road and railway networks are on par with those of the world’s most advanced economies and, in many ways, far superior to America’s.
But the Chinese economy is also deeply unbalanced, like a bodybuilder who has bulked up only his torso. Consumption, the primary growth engine in advanced economies, remains weak.

Eastern China has marquee cities that are well on their way to rivaling their Western counterparts, yet in many smaller cities and rural areas, home to at least half of China’s population, living standards fall somewhere between those of Latin America and South Asia.

The fear now is that, with its housing bubble having collapsed, China may never escape the so-called middle-income trap. When Japan’s real-estate crisis hit, it was already a very wealthy country, with per-capita income rivaling that of the US.

Thirty years later, its per-capita income is closer to Italy’s, which in turn is below that of Mississippi, the poorest US state. And China today is nowhere near as rich as Japan was in the early 1990s.

Between automation and AI, the most dynamic parts of China’s most dynamic sectors are not creating enough jobs. Youth unemployment has gotten so bad that authorities no longer publish the figures regularly.

Even under the best of circumstances, it would be difficult to replace the sagging real-estate and infrastructure sector, which, as Yang and I show, accounts for nearly one-third of demand once both direct and indirect effects are included.

Still, it would be wrong to assume that China’s real-estate crisis necessarily constrains its ability to compete geopolitically or economically. If you speak to businesspeople or attend tech conferences, you will hear that China’s economy is dominant and innovative.
China is not a democracy, and its leaders can allow the dynamic tech and export sectors to flourish even as the rest of the domestic economy takes decades to work off the overbuilding binge.

It is entirely possible to imagine 450 million Chinese people flourishing in a dynamic economy dominated by tech and manufacturing, while the other 950 million get by at a much lower standard of living.
Faced with such a divide, most Western democracies would be overwhelmed by pressure for redistribution, as European countries already know well.

But that need not be the case in China, particularly if the government believes that national security and the country’s global role depend on bolstering its frontier sectors. And 450 million people is still more than the US population and on par with that of the European Union.
Whether such an outcome is possible, of course, remains to be seen. Since Xi Jinping became president in 2013, the Communist Party has paid considerable attention to regional disparities.
But the economic forces that concentrate activity in major hubs, together with the strong desire to assert power internationally, may ultimately trump the pressure to reduce inequality.

The great economic historian Angus Maddison, writing in the late 1960s, argued that—contrary to the views of many economists, including Paul Samuelson—the Soviet Union would never fully catch up with the US. Nevertheless, thanks to its rich scientific tradition, the USSR could still compete at the technological frontier and achieve military parity.
One major difference between the Soviet Union and China is that China has bent over backwards to integrate with the US, both in trade and in science.
Despite US president Donald Trump’s trade war, it is clear that today’s challenges, from climate change to rogue AI, cannot be solved without extensive cooperation between the two superpowers.

So, as paralysing as China’s real-estate crisis has been, and even though excess construction will likely hold down growth for years to come, the dynamic core of its economy will keep thriving, so long as the country remains politically stable—and does not succumb to the temptations of imperial overreach.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund, is professor of economics and public policy at Harvard University and the recipient of the 2011 Deutsche Bank Prize in Financial Economics.

105bd5411c8476df: If you have any industrial smart freezers, look out. The US federal government is urging owners and operators to disconnect them from the internet, apply patches, change default passwords, and take other security measures to prevent the kind of attacks that have become prevalent in Europe.

“We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement.

Since mid-October, unknown miscreants have hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden. The attacks increase the temperature inside fridges to highs of 50ºC (122°F), spoiling food, and sparking fires.

The Register asked the FBI if it has documented any successful or attempted attacks against refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in America. We had not received a response to our questions at the time of publication, nor are we aware of any documented digital attacks against these systems in American supermarkets.
But there are signs that stateside operators are aware of the issue.

Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, last month said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack that affected most of its US and European brands.
Delhaize supermarkets in Europe are among those hit by the destructive freezer attacks.

The Pentagon is also reportedly treating a series of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the US in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to Reuters, which cited four officials familiar with the matter.

In a Thursday advisory, the US FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services, and departments of Agriculture and Transportation warned organizations about the ongoing cyber threats facing operators of industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies said.

Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds. Once criminals gain access to the systems, they can change the temperature to spoil food or temperature-controlled medications, start fires, and ultimately harm people who consume products that haven’t been stored at proper temperatures.
How to stay frosty

To prevent these scenarios, the government organizations urge owners and operators to “immediately” implement best practices and security protections. First and foremost on the list: do not expose industrial control systems and devices to the public internet.

Iranian hackers used internet-accessible programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to break into more than 100 US water systems in July. This sort of exposed device, which often lacks password protection, is a boon to miscreants looking for an easy button to gain access to critical facilities.
“Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities,” the feds advise.
Other recommended tactics include:
Create a dedicated VLAN for operational technology (OT) devices, to isolate industrial devices from business networks.
Replace default passwords with strong passwords and policies, turning on phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) whenever possible.
Apply patches in a timely manner, and retire and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates from the manufacturer.
Define and maintain a device and IP allow-list, and limit access to OT devices to only those on the list.
Maintain and test backups. These should be kept offsite and offline.
And finally: enable logging and regularly review logs for any unusual activity.®

581771537c149e57: LONDON: The Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in over three years on Thursday and warned that at least one more increase was likely if the US-Iran conflict continues, as it started on a path already begun by its main peers.

British inflation is likely to rise to around 5% in the middle of next year, the BoE said, more than double the central bank's target and a blow to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has sought to ease cost of living pressures.

The BoE found little evidence so far of faster inflation outside sectors directly hit by higher energy costs. However, policymakers said that the amount of inflation pressure coming down the road after months of high energy prices required a rate rise now, even though that will increase borrowing costs for businesses and many home owners.

"Today's increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. That is not inevitable. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase," Governor Andrew Bailey said in his opening remarks at a press conference.

Sterling strengthened against the US dollar after the decision. Two-year British government bond yields which are sensitive to expectations of future rate moves — rose while yields fell elsewhere, as investors increased bets on a back-to-back rate hike next month.
"December's meeting now looks like a coin flip, with the path of oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor," said Andrew Goodwin, chief UK economist at Oxford Economics.

The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to raise rates to 4% from 3.75%, the first rise since August 2023. In contrast to expectations in a Reuters poll, the dissent came not from a policymaker seeking to keep rates on hold but one seeking a bigger hike.
Catherine Mann, who said last month that the BoE had been slow to reassure markets that it had a grip on inflation, voted for a half-point interest rate increase to 4.25%.

Until now, the BoE had not followed the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and other central banks in raising rates in response to inflation pressures from the Iran war, arguing that the higher starting level of BoE rates made a hike less urgent.

Bailey said a big fall in oil prices over the last 48 hours — a move largely driven by the results of US midterm elections — was "encouraging news" but said previous falls in oil prices and of easing Middle East tensions had proven to be false dawns.
Moreover, he said a further rate hike was likely to be needed even if oil prices stayed at current levels as there was "already a significant amount of inflationary pressure in the pipeline".
British household energy bills are regulated under a formula which follows wholesale prices with around a three-month lag.
BOE predicts faster growth, higher inflation

In its central forecast for growth and inflation, the BoE revised up its expectations for growth this year and next to 1.6% and 1.3% respectively — notably stronger than the government's Office for Budget Responsibility predicted last week.

The upgrade follows strong official data this year, and the BoE attributed some of the strength to spending on artificial intelligence and a small, temporary boost from finance minister John Healey's annual budget last week.
However, after the effect of inflation and taxes, the average British household's income from work is set to fall both this year and next, the BoE said.

Under the BoE's central scenario, inflation does not return to its 2% target until the third quarter of 2028, six months later than the BoE predicted in July after a lull in the US-Iran conflict which had lowered energy costs.
The BoE now sees inflation peaking at 4.8% in the second quarter of next year, and said it would have been on course to top 5% without measures in Healey's budget.

In a more adverse scenario where oil prices peak near $130 a barrel, up from around US$100 currently, inflation hits 6.2% in the third quarter of 2027 – just under half the rate it hit in 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
d54b20a79ea20e81: AWS Kiro, the cloud giant's AI-oriented integrated development environment, isn't the most popular code editor.
That honor goes to Microsoft's Visual Studio Code, at least as measured by Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey.

Kiro might rank 27th among the listed IDEs, but then it's not really an IDE anymore. Having shrugged off reports that it played a role in outages last year, Kiro now styles itself "an agentic development environment" after a brief stint as "an agentic IDE."
It's also the inheritor of Amazon Q Developer coding assistant users, who have been directed to migrate to Kiro.

It's also "an AI-powered development environment that helps you build software from prototype to production." It's "available as a desktop IDE, a command-line interface, a web app, a mobile app, and a personal AI agent (Crew)."
Except that Kiro Crew is also "the persistent, open source development workspace." It's more agent infrastructure – an environment – that supports Kiro Web, IDE, and CLI.

To help get Kiro through its identity crisis and perhaps make it more beloved, AWS is expanding Kiro's remit still further. The cloud giant is launching Kiro Crew bots, recalling similar efforts like OpenAI dots and Grok Bot, as well as Claude Duet and Meta Muse.
Bots in Kiro Crew are software agents that attempt to carry out long-running tasks.
"A bot is a new way to structure and drive agentic work," a Kiro blog post explains.

"Instead of working in isolated sessions, each bot is a named, long-running agent that you define and customize for a specific part of your work. It has its own memory and runs its own sessions so you stop tracking them one by one. Kiro Crew already learns from how you work. Bots change where that learning lives."
There's some appealing anthropomorphism to giving each agent a name and its own tools, permissions, and memories. You're suddenly surrounded by friends.
The possible downside is how that gets billed – there's potential for a lot of duplicated context if your many agents process overlapping data without some form of shared cache.

Given Amazon's concerns about internal token usage and developer complaints about runaway costs in Kiro, it seems other organizations might be curious about the potential expense of keeping bot memory isolated.

In response to our inquiry about the cost of keeping memory separate, an AWS spokesperson said, “All of the Kiro bots bill together through a developer’s existing Kiro plan. Each bot in Kiro Crew has its own memory and sessions, and their learned context is intentionally kept separate so that what one bot learns doesn’t bleed into another’s work. However, all bots operate within the same Kiro Crew workspace, use the same harness, and have access to the same codebase, project files, MCP, skills, and tools—so they don’t need to independently rediscover your project structure.”

In any event, figuring out how Kiro Crew agents are spending tokens looks likely to require analytics of some sort, because AWS Kiro subscriptions are sold as "credits" that get converted to tokens at different rates, depending on the underlying model.
As a thought experiment, AWS suggests a developer might deploy an intake bot for reading trouble or job tickets, labeling them, flagging duplicates, and drafting reproduction steps for bugs.
Then there might be the build-health bot for checking the CI pipeline periodically and surfacing test failures that require the attention made scarce by having to deal with a bunch of AI agents.

A code review bot might also be warranted for reviewing pull requests and other delegated responsibilities. And top that off with a release-readiness bot, for confirming that merged changes have tests and for seeking release sign-off.
For those smitten by the idea of a single surface through which multiple agents can be configured, routed, and governed, Kiro Crew has your backend. ®

ff430ec6d234ec4f: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Following widespread backlash, Meta announced earlier this week it’s putting a planned update of its commercial terms of use on pause. If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

185aeeb9861ea879: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections. As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals, as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation. Wayne County voters The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black. After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide. About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms, up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot. In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes, which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County. Statewide support is holding steady In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3%, from 50.6% in 2020, as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris. Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote. In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues. Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden. Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024. While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll. Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed. NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson, who won the governorship over Republican John James. Historic power and unity Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement. Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate. However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity. Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates. Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination. If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns. My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations. An agenda that matters El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program, while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education. El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience. El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries. Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026. Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election. Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day. “I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers. Christine Slaughter does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
2cd0d025ccf2b230: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks.

News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool.
“The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email.

For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year.

The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent.

Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained.

According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said.

Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem.

“Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.”
In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while.

“Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.”

Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them.

Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems.

Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over.
“Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed.
The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

b2a9c85dded5b523: With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet.

While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star's light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope's configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets.

Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.

c61645b48e45a038: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Archaeologists have discovered the oldest direct evidence of psychoactive cannabis use in a Siberian tomb that dates back 2,800 years and was the site of human and horse sacrifices, according to a study published on Thursday in Science.

During excavations of the tomb, a team found more than 1,400 cannabis seeds scattered around the remains of several Iron Age individuals, and even identified cannabinoids—including the active compound tetrahydrocannabinol (THC)—in a person’s preserved hair.

Though humans cultivated cannabis for many millennia before the Iron Age, this is by far the earliest clear-cut proof that the plant was consumed for its psychoactive effects, which have made it one of the most widely used drugs in the world today.

The discovery is “absolutely crazy,” said Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology and the University of Bern who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. “People have been speculating a lot about psychoactive use of cannabis in the past, but to actually pin it down and prove it with soft tissue evidence of the humans involved—that is something very special.
“That is an absolutely unique and extremely rare combination of evidence,” he added.

Cannabis has a multifaceted history as a recreational drug and a pop cultural touchstone, as well as a traditional medicine that has been used for millennia by many cultures, including in China, Russia, and around the Mediterranean Basin. Humans began cultivating the plant as early as 10,000 years ago for its oil and fiber, but the origins of its specific consumption as a psychoactive substance is unclear.

Cannabis was important to the Scythian culture, a horse-riding people that emerged on the Eurasian steppes in the 9th century BCE and became a major force in the subsequent centuries. The historian Herodotus described Scythian rituals that involved ceremonial burning of cannabis in enclosed spaces, and their cannabis residues and products have been found at Scythian archaeological sites.

“Herodotus speaks about the Scythians being quite fond of cannabis in the first place, so this has always been in the back of our minds,” Caspari said. “But it is so incredibly rare to find well-preserved plant remains that this is not really something you can hope for or look for. This is ultimately complete luck and chance.”

Now, Caspari and his colleagues have hit an archaeological jackpot at a tomb known as Tunnug 1, located in Siberia’s Uyuk River Valley. Six elite individuals are interred in the interior of the royal mound inside several tree-trunk coffins and wooden structures. They are mostly men, though one woman is also present. The mound is lined with remains of sacrificed humans, as well as dozens of sacrificed horses, close to the surface.

As the team carefully worked through the layers of the burial, they found hundreds of cannabis seeds distributed around the bodies that were dated to the 8th century BCE. However, the real smoking blunt was the detection of cannabinols in preserved hair samples, including traces of THC, the most important mind-altering compound in cannabis.

The results confirm contemporaneous accounts of Scythians as cannabis consumers who used the plant for purification and mortuary rituals. It’s possible that the people selected as human sacrifice consumed the drug to prepare them for their unenviable fate.

“It being in a burial context, of course, there's a ritual aspect to it,” Caspari explained. “It might be a little bit more sinister, but this is speculation. We do have a lot of horse sacrifices and also some human sacrifices on the surface of the mound. And if you imagine humans being sacrificed, they usually don't like that very much. It might be advantageous to have them dosed a little bit, at least, to make the procedure a bit more humane, if you will.”
“Of course, that is speculation,” he cautioned. “We don't have any written sources about that particular area, but that's at least one way we could go with our interpretation.”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The researchers hope to learn more about the context and meaning of the cannabis use at Tunnug 1 through continued excavations and an analysis of more hair samples. What’s more, the team plans to conduct DNA analysis on the seeds, an approach that could yield new insights about the murky history of cannabis domestication and its early use as a psychoactive substance. This line of research could also shed light on modern cannabis strains, and may even be revived for new medicinal or recreational purposes.

“We've already sequenced part of the seeds to unravel and disentangle the domestication history,” Caspari said. “Funnily enough, we don't even know what wild cannabis actually looks like because there has been so much intermixing and interbreeding since the 70s, when people started experimenting and trying to get more potent drug variants. Some of the initial landraces and the actual wild cannabis has been lost.”

“Now, having DNA that's almost 3,000 years old, we will be able to take that step back into the past and see what an unaltered cannabis would have looked like,” he said. “In the ideal case, we might even be able to work together with the medical industry and bring some of these very ancient genetics back into cannabis production to potentially help people with very interesting and distinctive cannabinoid combinations.”

Put that in your pipe and smoke it. Regardless of where future research into this ancient plant leads, this long-sought evidence of cannabis use thousands of years ago confirms the rich cultural legacy of the plant across time and space.

“As an archeologist, I might be a bit biased here, but I think the history and cultural practices really do matter,” Caspari concluded. “I think our findings do indeed inform current discussions on legalization, on usage of medical cannabis—which is very much an ongoing discourse—and I think what we've been able to do with this study is provide an anchor, and show that there is this deep cultural history to the use of cannabis as a psychoactive drug.”

9db2ee442db69062: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions.

The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled.

If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration.
That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not.

Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration.
The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually.

In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account.

Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out.

The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk.

Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going.

In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times.

On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack.

Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set.

There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®
