cecdb40ec5b3ec06: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 5 — Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has decided to maintain the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) at 2.75 per cent following its final Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting of the year today.
In a statement, the central bank said the latest indicators pointed to continued resilience in global growth, supported by strong global technology investment and stable labour markets.
“At the current OPR level, the MPC considers the monetary policy stance to be consistent with the outlook of continued price stability and sustainable economic growth,” it said.
BNM said the MPC would remain vigilant to evolving conditions and assess their implications for the balance of risks surrounding the outlook for domestic inflation and economic growth.
Year-to-date, headline and core inflation averaged 1.8 per cent and 1.9 per cent, respectively, the central bank said.
Looking ahead to 2027, geopolitical developments, elevated global commodity prices and adverse weather conditions are expected to exert upward pressure on inflation.
Both headline and core inflation are therefore expected to edge higher, although they are likely to remain contained amid continued domestic policy measures and stable demand conditions.
“The MPC will remain vigilant to cost pressures and domestic demand conditions given their impact on the inflation outlook,” BNM said.
Inflation has edged higher following an increase in energy costs and is expected to remain elevated as higher costs continue to be passed through to consumer prices.

On the global outlook, BNM said uncertainties surrounding geopolitical developments would continue to weigh on growth and fuel inflationary pressures. However, the impact is expected to be cushioned by sustained technology-related spending and continued adaptation to supply constraints.

Downside risks to global growth include prolonged geopolitical tensions, tighter global financial conditions arising from monetary policy adjustments, concerns over financial market valuations and fiscal vulnerabilities.
“Upside potential could come from stronger technology spending and a faster-than-expected recovery in supply chain conditions,” the central bank said.
On the domestic front, recent indicators point to continued strength in economic growth in the third quarter of 2026, underpinned by robust exports and sustained domestic demand.
The solid momentum is expected to lift full-year growth in 2026 to above five per cent.
“Looking ahead, the economy’s sound fundamentals are expected to keep growth resilient in 2027.
“The external sector is expected to remain a major driver of growth, supported by the ongoing global technology upcycle and firm tourist spending,” BNM said.
Stable labour market conditions and continued investment activity are also expected to support domestic demand, while measures under Budget 2027 will provide further impetus to private consumption.
However, the growth outlook remains subject to downside risks, including a prolonged conflict in the Middle East and lower commodity production.
On the upside, stronger-than-expected global growth, firmer technology-related export demand and higher tourism activity could provide additional support to economic expansion, BNM added. — Bernama
22b3559c44474108: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 5 — Malaysia stood out in Southeast Asia’s initial public offering (IPO) market in the first nine months of 2026, accounting for 38 of the 56 listings recorded across the region, according to Ernst & Young (EY).

The 38 IPOs raised US$1.62 billion (RM6.56 billion, based on US$1=RM4.05), compared with US$992 million (RM4.02 billion) raised through 37 listings in the corresponding period last year, stated EY in a factsheet today.

In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026), Malaysia recorded nine IPOs raising US$167.2 million (RM677.2 million), compared with eight IPOs that raised US$94 million (RM380.7 million) in the same quarter last year.

Among other Southeast Asian markets, Singapore recorded eight IPOs raising US$1.28 billion (RM5.18 billion), followed by Indonesia with seven IPOs raising US$121.3 million (RM491.3 million) and Thailand with three IPOs raising US$21.3 million (RM86.3 million).
Southeast Asia recorded 56 IPOs raising US$3 billion (RM12.15 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, a decline of 26 per cent in volume and 13 per cent in value year-on-year.
In 3Q 2026, 20 IPOs raised US$500 million (RM2.03 billion), compared with 26 IPOs that raised US$2.1 billion (RM8.51 billion) over the same period in 2025.
EY Capital Markets representative Nghia Trung Nguyen said Malaysia exceeded both the number of listings and proceeds recorded over the same period last year.
“The stronger proceeds are encouraging and point to continued investor appetite for quality companies with compelling growth prospects.

“This momentum also reflects the role of the capital market in supporting companies as they pursue their next phase of growth, providing access to capital while broadening their investor base and market profile,” he said in a statement.
Nghia said issuers needed to be well-prepared and realistic about market timing and investor expectations amid an uncertain global environment, as investors became increasingly selective.

He added that a compelling business proposition, supported by strong fundamentals, good governance and a clear growth strategy, remained crucial to securing a successful listing and sustaining investor confidence beyond the IPO.

EY Asean IPO leader Chan Yew Kiang said regulatory reforms, a muted economic outlook and geopolitical uncertainties had dampened listing sentiment across the region, prompting IPO aspirants to adopt a more cautious approach.

“Hence, in 3Q 2026, except Malaysia, IPO transaction counts across Southeast Asia slowed compared with the same period last year. Exchanges in the region also began to focus on unlocking shareholders’ value through different initiatives.

“For example, in Singapore, while the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) that was introduced in February 2025 had injected liquidity and vibrancy into the local exchanges, more needs to be done by corporates to improve liquidity and post-IPO performance,” he said.

Globally, EY said there were 908 IPOs that raised US$290 billion (RM1.17 trillion) in the first nine months of 2026, representing a two per cent decline in deal volume but a 153 per cent increase in proceeds compared with the corresponding period in 2025.
It said for 3Q 2026, there were 387 IPOs that raised US$95.6 billion (RM387.2 billion), compared with 374 IPOs that raised US$52 billion (RM210.6 billion) over the same period in 2025.

In terms of regional performance, EY said Asia-Pacific recorded 399 IPOs raising US$93.2 billion (RM377.5 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 14 per cent in volume and 79 per cent in proceeds year-on-year.

Meanwhile, the Europe, Middle East, India and Africa (EMEIA) region recorded 389 IPOs raising US$30.2 billion (RM122.3 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, representing a one per cent increase in volume and six per cent in proceeds year-on-year.

According to EY, Americas’ IPO activity saw a 35 per cent decline in deal volume to 120 listings in the first nine months of 2026, although proceeds surged 392 per cent to US$166.6 billion (RM674.7 billion). — Bernama

cf403874a276142d: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?

e8bf6269fd8b236d: Anna Moneymaker/Getty The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections puts them in a stronger position to interfere with President Donald Trump’s agenda. This includes his deeply unpopular and costly war against Iran, which could be among their first priorities. As president, Trump will be able to veto any legislation aimed at ending the war. But the Democrats still have another powerful card up their sleeves: cutting off funding for the war. There are caveats, however. History suggests exercising this power could trigger a political confrontation that may backfire. And even if the Democrats succeed in ending the war, they may not be able to reverse the damage it has done to the US’ global standing. The limits of legislation Democrats will have three main options to try to force the war against Iran to a close. Two of these, however, face significant limitations. The first – and perhaps most obvious – option is through legislation. There are a few different ways to do this. One approach is to pass a resolution calling for an end to the war. Congress already attempted this in June, passing a concurrent resolution (with the support of some Republicans) that directed the president to either withdraw US forces from hostilities against Iran or seek the approval of Congress before continuing. This was done under the War Powers Resolution of 1973. These so-called concurrent resolutions are, however, widely seen as non-binding. Intended to express the opinion or will of Congress, they are generally used to deal with internal matters within Congress. Trump ignored it. A similar resolution then failed in the Senate in September. For such a resolution to be binding, it would need the force of a law passed by Congress, which the president would likely veto. To overcome that veto, the Democrats would need the support of a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This would require a significant number of Republicans to cross the aisle. Exercising oversight A second option for the Democrats is to launch a series of congressional investigations into the way the war has been conducted. This would likely include public hearings, subpoenas and demands for documents from the Trump administration. The Democrats may also attempt to impeach senior officials in the Trump administration. If Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat tipped to become the next speaker of the House, wants to appease some of the more progressive voices in his party – or the hardline voices on the Iran war or against Trump – Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be targeted for impeachment. But the grounds for such proceedings are unclear at this stage, and even with the Democrats’ new Senate majority, he would be unlikely to be convicted unless a significant number of Republicans crossed the aisle. More pertinently, congressional investigations are a protracted process, and unlikely to bring the war to a swift end. The ‘power of the purse’ The more immediate power that Congress has to end the war swiftly is in Article I, Section 9 of the US Constitution, which states: No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law […] This is known as the “power of the purse”. Once the new Congress is sworn in in January, every new dollar that Trump’s Department of War wants to spend needs to be approved by the House and the Senate. A Democrat-controlled Congress could put a clause into the defence budget, prohibiting funds from being used for hostilities against Iran. Trump could veto this, but this would mean blocking the paycheck for everyone in the military, as well. The Democrats tried this very approach in 2007, attempting to force a timetable for a US withdrawal from Iraq. Then-President George W. Bush vetoed it, but it became a political football, with both sides accusing the other of leaving US troops unfunded. The Democrats ultimately backed down due to the growing risk of backlash from voters. Today, this approach would carry a similar risk. Are the Democrats willing to put their political credibility on the line if the president accuses them of letting American soldiers down? Who blinks first? Republicans face a reckoning As the dust settled on Wednesday, Trump himself acknowledged the Iran war had played a role in the Republican Party’s crushing defeat. But he doubled down on the decision, saying he would do it all over again if necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Vice President JD Vance was less defensive. In a detailed statement posted to X, Vance bluntly declared the war was the reason the Republicans lost. He added, “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there”. Vance has long criticised US military involvement in overseas conflicts, but in his role as vice president has publicly backed Trump’s actions against Iran. This week’s overwhelming Democratic victory has made it much easier for Vance – and other Republicans – to now break ranks with the president. The balance of power has shifted For Trump, bringing the war to an end now would mean humiliation. The US has so far poured almost US$50 billion into a military campaign with few tangible achievements. On top of that, Iran has learned that the Strait of Hormuz is a chokepoint it can control. The same is true for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait off the coast of Yemen, where the Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked commercial ships. These costs will outlast the Trump presidency. The war might definitively bring to an end the unipolar global order Washington built after the end of the Cold War. The biggest winner may not be Tehran, but Beijing. Markus Wagner received funding from the Australian Department of Defence as principal investigator for the Weaponised Trade project.

16de4ca3c25d3eed: In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device. This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifies entries in a robot’s memory that might be wrong and corrects the descriptions of mislabeled objects.  In the future, this method could make household or industrial robots better able to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as clearing a dining room table or working alongside human collaborators to assemble a piece of machinery.  Called UQ-DAAAM (which stands for Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), the system compares multiple descriptions of the same object, seen from different viewpoints, to quantify the robot’s uncertainty about what it saw.  It then selects additional views to reduce the uncertainty and combines these captions into a more accurate description of the object, which it saves to memory. The researchers also employed a special technique to streamline this process so a mobile robot can continually update uncertain memory entries in real time.  When compared to baseline methods, UQ-DAAAM boosted the robot’s confidence and improved the accuracy of its answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when it saw them.  “Contrary to ChatGPT, when we think about physical AI, it is not enough to simply put a disclaimer cautioning that sometimes the robot might be wrong. Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro), principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), director of the MIT SPARK Laboratory, and the senior author of the paper presenting UQ-DAAAM. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Harry Zhang and Nicolas Gorlo. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  Amending memory This new method builds on the researchers’ prior work, DAAAM, a robot memory system that uses a vision-language model (VLM) to richly describe objects in scenes a robot captures with its onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored as detailed captions in a 3D map-based representation of the robot’s environment that it can call upon later to answer questions.  But the robot sometimes sees objects only partially or from far away, or its camera might capture blurry or poorly lit images. In these cases, DAAAM might describe these objects incorrectly, such as by mistaking a gray chimney for a squirrel perched on a rooftop. “With no way to correct itself, this wrong memory would persist as the robot proceeds in its environment, which could impact downstream applications,” Zhang says. UQ-DAAAM integrates uncertainty quantification into the DAAAM framework. It allows the robot to measure its confidence in the accuracy of object descriptions and fix incorrect captions as it travels through an environment. While on the move, the robot constantly collects and stores images of the world around it. Many of these images show the same objects captured from different angles. UQ-DAAAM uses these additional viewpoints to identify and correct unreliable descriptions. First, it calculates the VLM’s confidence level in the words it generated to describe a potentially mislabeled object. Then, it measures consistency by comparing this description to captions of images that describe the same object from different vantage points. “We fuse both sources of uncertainty into a single number that captures how certain the VLM is in its overall understanding of the object,” Carlone explains. If that number exceeds a certain threshold, the uncertainty is too high, and UQ-DAAAM will refine the caption by using additional images of the object. It does this using a heuristic, or simple rule, that determines which additional viewpoints will reduce the robot’s uncertainty about the object. For instance, it might choose an image captured a few frames later that clearly shows smoke emanating from the chimney.  The researchers mathematically proved that this heuristic can identify the best frames to select without rerunning the VLM, dramatically reducing the amount of computation.  “The key challenge Nico and Harry had to overcome is how to combine VLMs with uncertainty quantification into something that is running in a fraction of a second on a robot that is moving,” Carlone says. Remembering with confidence Once it has identified additional captions that will reduce its uncertainty about the object, the system uses an LLM to fuse them into a single object description. To boost accuracy, the LLM puts more weight on new captions and those with less ambiguity. This refinement step is able to resolve ambiguities for about 92 percent of the objects in the robot’s environment, while only requiring two additional captions per object. It increased the accuracy of object descriptions by 5 percent compared to the state of the art. UQ-DAAAM also provided more accurate answers to questions about the objects it observed, where it saw them, and when it last encountered them than baseline methods. “Performing this uncertainty quantification procedure across the entire map the robot generates allows it to improve its understanding of what it has observed,” Gorlo says. Next, the researchers want to use UQ-DAAAM to guide different types of robots, like mobile robotic manipulators, and apply their uncertainty quantification techniques to other domains.  In addition, they are studying the use of UQ-DAAAM to identify areas of high uncertainty the robot could revisit to improve its understanding of the environment. They are also exploring uncertainty quantification in systems that predict the future state of a robot’s environment. This research is supported, in part, by the U.S. Army Research Laboratory and the U.S. Office of Naval Research. Carlone is currently on sabbatical as an Amazon Scholar; this article describes work performed at MIT and is not associated with Amazon.
2e0612d18143103c: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

1c5f8252381c9e95: Menurut ahli falsafah dan sejarawan Perancis yang terkenal, Pierre Nora; terdapat satu hubungan erat antara sejarah dan memori. Akan tetapi Nora menegaskan, dalam banyak keadaan memori adalah lebih utama dan dalam banyak keadaan mengatasi sejarah. Ini kerana memori adalah pencarian kebenaran yang objektif a search for objective truth atau satu himpunan bagaimana ia pernah terjadi, a recollection of how it really was.

Sedangkan sejarah tidak sebebas memori, dan kadangkala perlu dikendala. Ini kerana sejarah selalunya mempunyai aspek ideologi dan boleh dimanipulasi, ideological and manipulative. Idea dan gagasan Nora mengenai pertentangan memori melawan sejarah ini boleh ditemukan dalam banyak karya-karya beliau, antara lain The Present. Nation. Memory; Between Memory and History. Problems of Memory Places; World Celebration of Memory; History as Protection from Politics; dan dalam kerja beliau yang paling masyhur, Places of Memory.

Mengapakah Nora lebih berpihak kepada memori berbanding sejarah, sedang beliau adalah seorang sejarawan? Menurut Nora, beliau pertamanya ingin meluruskan semula sejarah dengan membersihkannya dari fakta tertentu.

Fakta-fakta sejarah ini pada Nora telah dimanipulasi oleh agenda politik dan hanya memori secara kolektif yang dapat membetulkan keadaan ini. Nora dalam kerja-kerja akademiknya menyorot bagaimana gerakan politik, pengukuhan identiti kebangsaan Perancis, dan agenda kelompok tertentu boleh mencemarkan sejarah. Tugas sejarawan sebenarnya adalah memelihara atau melindungi memori ini.

Atas alasan inilah Nora melancarkan gagasan beliau yang dikenali sebagai Places of Memory. Bagaimanapun cabaran untuk meluruskan sejarah dengan mencari memori yang benar ini bukanlah mudah, memandangkan memori itu sendiri terputus, tambahan pula tradisi sendiri akan hancur atau ditinggalkan, dan inovasi mengambil tempat sehingga memori kolektif itu sendiri ikut terjejas. Nora menyatakan, memori yang benar hanya datang dari ruang-tempat memori berjejak memory places atau mnemonic places, yang hadir membentuk ruang memori.

Nora menafsirkan konsep places of memory (lieu de memoire) ini sebagai satu fenomena yang signifikan, terzahir ketara atau tidak ketara, yang mana kerana kenekadan masyarakat atau pengaruh zaman telah membentuk sebagai satu lambang warisan untuk bangsa;

Memori kolektif terbentuk oleh kerana memori berjejak ini yang termanifestasi secara benda, fungsi dan lambang. Memori berjejak dalam bentuk benda misalnya adalah monumen, tugu, memorial, perkabungan, penyanjungan, wajah pada stem atau duit kertas, acara yang bersempenakan memori ini, nama jalan; dan lain-lain. Memori yang terputus memerlukan memori berjejak ini supaya dapat diingat kembali dan sekaligus dimurnikan semula sejarahnya. Sesuatu hanya ‘menjadi sejarah setelah memori berakhir, selagi memori dipugar secara kolektif maka sesuatu itu belum menjadi sejarah meskipun sudah berlaku pada masa lampau’; dalam erti kata lain ‘sejarah akan terus hidup jika terus dikenang’.

Harus diingat, memori berjejak Nora selalu dikelirukan oleh ramai sebagai satu tempat, ini kerana terjemahan suntuk place of memory itu dikait dengan physical place, padahal ia telah kehilangan tempat dan lebih kepada simbol atau tanda, kesan, atau jejak.

Saya selalu mengangankan, atau mencita-citakan agar nama Wan Azizah Wan Ismail terlekat dalam memori Malaysia, di saat beliau masih bernafas dan masih hidup. Beliau memiliki tempat dalam memori negara. Saya khuatir meletakkannya dalam sejarah. Ini kerana seperti mana dilihat oleh Nora, sejarah boleh mengalami pemesongan. Buku sejarah boleh diubah oleh pihak yang menang. Sejarah boleh dipadam. Tetapi memori misalnya tidak boleh dipadam. Yazid bin Muawiyah sebagai contoh cuba memadam sejarah mengenai cucu Rasulullah. Dia gagal. Ini kerana Zaynab al Kubra, puteri Fatimah dan Saidina Ali menghidupkan memori abangnya itu dengan segar dan harum. Ia menjadikan kesyahidan itu sentiasa hidup.

Sejarah telah membuktikan bahawa wanita di alam Melayu bukanlah kelompok yang pasif atau hanya berdiri di belakang kejayaan seseorang pimpinan masyarakat. Antara fakta dari lipatan sejarah alam Melayu, dapat dikenali sosok seorang Permaisuri bernama Pramodawardhana yang bertanggungjawab di belakang Kerajaan Majapahit dan Pembangunan Borobudur yang inklusif. Dari era kesultanan hingga ke zaman perjuangan kemerdekaan dan era pemodenan dan digital masa kini, wanita Melayu telah memainkan peranan yang amat signifikan sebagai pemimpin, diplomat, pendidik, usahawan, pemikir sosiobudaya, dan tiang seri utama dalam keharmonian nusa bangsa.

Di saat berlakunya krisis dalam masyarakat, wanita terbukti menjadi penyelamat. Seperti dilakukan oleh Tengku Ampuan Intan Tengku Alang Hussain yang menjadi Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan antara tahun 1869-1872 iaitu ketika berlakunya pertelingkahan untuk merebut kuasa. Watak sedemikian muncul lagi di zaman kita, dengan nama Wan Azizah Wan Ismail.

Selaku timbalan perdana menteri (2018-2020) dan pemimpin di Kementerian Pembangunan Wanita, Keluarga dan Masyarakat (KPWKM), Wan Azizah ketika itu telah melancarkan Pelan Tindakan Kebangsaan Menangani Punca Perkahwinan Bawah Umur (2020-2025). Pelan ini merangkumi strategi menyeluruh berasaskan lima punca utama yang digariskan menerusi kajian mendalam, iaitu kemiskinan sosioekonomi, kekurangan akses kepada pendidikan, kepincangan maklumat kesihatan reproduktif, kelonggaran undang-undang, serta persepsi dan stigma masyarakat. Saya membayangkan bagaimana kiranya memori Wan Azizah ini disuburkan terus. Dan memori itu diberi nyawa apabila lima punca di atas terus dikaji dan diberi solusi oleh sebuah universiti. Kita ahli akademik mengkaji dan memberi solusi, atas nama Wan Azizah. Berbahagi pahala.

Satu lagi tonggak utama dalam perjuangan pemerkasaan wanita yang sentiasa Wan Azizah tekankan ialah pengiktirafan terhadap golongan suri rumah yang memerlukan perlindungan keselamatan sosial yang sewajarnya. Di tangan beliau lahir program i-Suri dan i-Sayang yang hari ini mesti diteruskan sebagai usaha menangani jurang perlindungan sosial. Kerajaan ketika itu melancarkan Skim i-Suri di bawah Caruman Sukarela Insentif Suri bagi memastikan suri rumah berdaftar dalam sistem eKasih mendapat tabungan hari tua di Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja (KWSP) dengan bantuan insentif kerajaan.

Memori atau legasi kerja bekas timbalan perdana menteri ini mesti dibaja. Ia mesti diberi, bak kata Pierre Nora, sebuah tanah pamah, sebuah watan dan tekad yang dapat menampang places of memory (lieu de memoire) tersebut. Kalau ada rezeki harapnya memori Wan Azizah ini akan dapat ditegakkan di kala beliau masih hidup, dan di kala saya masih berkhidmat sebagai ahli akademik.
Ini hanyalah angan-angan saya. Agar nama Wan Azizah itu abadi, dan mengatasi sejarah. Ia boleh dan Insya-Allah menjadi memori, satu kenangan yang wangi dan lama. Biarkan ia abadi.

36d4af5b6e476e47: From Clement Stanley
Malaysian Indian People’s Party, a Perikatan Nasional component, decided to skip the Melaka state election as a matter of principle, or so they say.
MIPP president P Punithan said the party would not compromise its principles simply to secure seats in the Nov 14 polls.

MIPP’s struggle, he declares, is to defend the interests of the Indian community with dignity and principles, and “that the community’s voice and interests deserve proper recognition and representation in the political landscape”.
In short, MIPP likely does not want to be seen as token for the opposition coalition’s supposed inclusiveness.
Which, in essence is fine. After all, how can a party market itself as an outfit that champions the Indian cause when it finds itself marginalised?
It is just horrible branding — apart from the fact they lost their deposits in the Johor election — which could be a factor as to why seat negotiations failed.
Yet, MIPP’s dilemma is also, to a certain extent, MIC’s.
What role does MIC play in the bigger scheme of things with respect to its affiliation with Barisan Nasional?
Would MIC be willing to accept the fact that it is by and large irrelevant and a “diversity hire” of sorts?
Are they content being pliant to Umno, BN’s lynchpin, since such an arrangement may guarantee a government post?
Or will they only display bravado, via empty threats to quit BN, before the party’s AGM?
To MIPP’s credit, they were brave to acknowledge where they stand in PN. It is now time for the MIC to do the same.
Pliancy and bravado, however, also bring us to MCA.
Mocked as being Umno’s lapdog for the longest time, MCA leaders walked out of BN’s candidate announcement over seat allocations, also over principles.

The party, its president Wee Ka Siong said, cannot be pushed around and deserves to be treated with dignity. Wee also later called out BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on his claim that talks held after the walkout were “positive”.
Whether one believes it was just “wayang kulit”, the bravado eventually secured three seats for MCA to contest at the Melaka election.
But can MCA consider this a win?
The optics will definitely boost its morale.
Perhaps this will give MCA something to build on. Perhaps they believe that by riding on the tailcoats of a BN-PN pact they will win over more Chinese support for the party.
But truth be told, their victory would be somewhat hollow if they won based on the support of the non-Chinese voters.
Be that as it may, MCA must surely know they are no force to be reckoned with amongst the Chinese electorate.
But, if survival is the name of the game, then by all means be indebted to the Malay support for putting them back in a position of power in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now very likely, in Melaka.
MCA now need only ask themselves, “How high?” when told to jump by the likes of Umno and PAS.
Clement Stanley is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
48faba62e27383cb: Voters cast their ballots at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. AP Photo/Yuki IwamuraThe crucial test for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate how voters are likely to decide. By that fundamental measure, the 2026 midterm polls largely succeeded in anticipating outcomes on Election Day. If somewhat tentatively, the polls overall had been signaling important gains for Democrats. And that is what voting produced. It was, perhaps, polling’s most reassuring performance since accurately anticipating Barack Obama’s presidential election in 2008, an outcome cited in my book, “Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in U.S. Presidential Elections.” Two truisms confirmed This is not to say the 2026 preelection polls offered precision estimates before returns poured in. They appear to have underestimated support for Democratic candidates in some Senate races. But spot-on precision, while enviable, is not what polls can be expected to produce, considering the many ways error can infiltrate opinion surveys. Given their checkered record in recent national elections, pollsters and media analysts tended to couch their end-of-campaign assessments in measured tentativeness. For example, Nate Cohn, chief political analyst for The New York Times, wrote just before the election that “it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. This is a real possibility. President Trump’s supporters are relatively unlikely to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.” That risk was mostly unrealized, as Republican candidates were swept in a red wipeout. The 2026 polls tended to confirm the truism in American politics that midterms typically are rough on candidates of the party that holds the presidency. Another truism, again reaffirmed, is that a president’s approval ratings often are useful in gauging the country’s mood before midterm elections. President Donald Trump’s preelection approval ratings hovered at or below 40%, according to survey data compiled by RealClearPolitics. Voters cast their ballots at the Bridge of Hope Church in Youngstown, Ohio, on Nov. 3, 2026. Jeff Swensen/Getty Images The U.S. war with Iran, launched by Trump, was a major factor propelling the unenviable ratings. The conflict went unresolved while fuel prices surged, bringing pain to consumers. Those and other problems prompted polling analyst Nate Silver to write that Trump “almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms. And the one superpower he has – turning out low-propensity voters in presidential years, the sorts of voters who apparently are often missed by pollsters – has never really worked when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot.” And it didn’t work this time, either, even though throughout the campaign Trump encouraged supporters to pretend his name was on the ballot and turn out to vote. Few polling misses When examined closely, the polls delivered some disagreement in the days before the election. Pollsters offered ranges that, in some races, were sizable. For example, was Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton up by 1 percentage point in Texas late in the campaign, or was he down 7 points? Paxton lost by double digits to Democrat James Talarico, a margin that no pollster anticipated. Similarly, was long-serving Republican Sen. Susan Collins ahead by 2 points in Maine or was she losing by 9 points? The outcome was closer to the latter reading, with Democrat Troy Jackson winning by more than six points. In Minnesota, was Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan up by 14 points, or by just 2 points? With most votes counted by the day after the election, Flanagan’s margin of victory was about 10 points. Such polling gaps in high-profile races offer a reminder to not focus on any single survey but, instead, to consider overall polling averages, which tend to remove or reduce the effects of outliers. None of this necessarily is to declare that pollsters have resolved their persistent problems in sampling, especially in interviewing hard-to-reach voters. But big polling misses like that in the Texas governor’s race – where Democrat Gina Hinojosa won by double digits, although polls had shown Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ahead by a few points – were few this election cycle. Meanwhile, the electorate’s broad inclinations were plainly if not precisely depicted. That outcome has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-beleaguered and much-criticized cohort. a40b144ab5da56eb: From a layperson’s perspective, following the legal back-and-forth in the Malaysian courts can be rather taxing.
It often appears to be a war of words, legal arguments, constitutional interpretations and courtroom strategies, all aimed at persuading the presiding judge or judges.

Beneath the pomp and pageantry inherited from the British legal system, however, lie issues of profound constitutional significance that may or may not affect our lives today, but could have far-reaching consequences for generations to come.

When Malaysia was formed in 1963, several safeguards were negotiated to protect the interests and autonomy of North Borneo (now Sabah). Among these was Point 11 of the Inter-Governmental Committee (IGC) Report, under the heading tariffs and finance.
It provided that “North Borneo should retain control over its own finances, development and tariffs, with the right to formulate its own taxation policies and raise loans on its own credit”.

One can argue that the spirit and substance of this safeguard are found in the constitutional expression of Article 112C of the Federal Constitution, read together with Section 2(1) of Part IV of the Tenth Schedule and Clauses (1), (3) and (4) of Article 112D.

These provisions form the constitutional basis for Sabah's entitlement to a special grant equivalent to two-fifths (40%) of the net revenue derived by the federal government from Sabah, subject to the relevant constitutional provisions.

Former Sabah minister Yap Pak Leong revived the historical significance of this arrangement, maintaining that the 40% revenue-sharing arrangement was a fundamental condition underpinning Sabah's decision to join in the formation of Malaysia.
"Right from the start, I emphasised this share of 2/5 revenue to be a condition for Sabah to become part of Malaysia.”
He further stressed that without this safeguard being enshrined in the Federal Constitution, Sabah would not have agreed to participate in the formation of Malaysia.

The role Sabah and Sarawak played in forming Malaysia must be recognised, unlike the federated states of Malaya. The Borneo states negotiated separate terms under the IGC, one of which is Sabah’s entitlement to 40% revenue sharing of all taxes collected in Sabah.

From what I understand, the federal government is not objecting to Sabah’s right to the 40% revenue sharing, but to the High Court judgment on Oct 17, 2025, in favour of the Sabah Law Society (SLS), directing the federal and state government to commence a review within a stipulated period.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself promised during the last state election that the government would not appeal the High Court’s decision, but for whatever reasons, it seems he has reneged on that promise to the Sabah people.
On another point, one cannot help but question the position taken by the state government in these proceedings.
Having entered the case as an intervener at a relatively late stage, the state government appears caught between competing legal and political considerations.
Yet, arguably, it should have been at the forefront pursuing Sabah's constitutional entitlement.
The state government possesses the political mandate, institutional authority and constitutional standing to negotiate directly with the federal government.

Rather than allowing the matter to become an extended courtroom battle initiated by SLS on behalf of the people of Sabah, it should be exercising that authority to secure a meaningful and just resolution for Sabah's 47 "lost years".

In another case, another NGO, Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (Sabar) has taken the federal government to court on February 27, 2025, disputing the validity of the Territorial Sea Act (TSA) 2012, which limits the State's maritime boundary to just three nautical miles.

While the Sabah state government may have its own reasons for not initiating legal challenges regarding Sabah's rights, and Sabahans are not privy to their arguments, it is only fair to ask where the Sabah government stands in relation to these key court challenges.
The position is unlike in Sarawak, where the state government has led similar challenges.

Importantly, after more than six decades since Sabah agreed to become a part of Malaysia, one uncomfortable reality remains: according to official statistics, Sabah continues to record the highest poverty incidence in the country.
That is a sobering indictment of the development gap that persists despite Sabah's immense natural resources and its contributions to the Malaysian federation.
The legal arguments may continue. Appeals may be filed, constitutional provisions may be debated, and lawyers may argue over jurisdiction, procedures and remedies.
But beyond the courtroom, ordinary Sabahans continue to face the realities of poverty, inadequate infrastructure, water and electricity shortages, and limited economic opportunities.

The fundamental question is this: after more than 60 years in the Malaysian federation, should Sabahans still have to fight in court for constitutional assurances that were meant to protect their interests from the very beginning?

The 40% entitlement should not be treated as a political bargaining chip, nor should its fulfilment be reduced to a battle of legal technicalities. It is a constitutional matter rooted in the historical terms and safeguards surrounding the formation of Malaysia.
It is about justice, constitutional accountability and the future of Sabah.
The people of Sabah have waited long enough. Following Lord Hewart CJ’s well-known dictum, “justice must be seen to be done”.

c6b1da594a8a831d: Over 60% of Floridian voters voted to cut property taxes, which has been surging in recent years. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes. Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis. But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments. While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off. How Amendment 3 would work Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes. In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses. So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters. Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits. But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached. Who pays the bill? Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments. With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups. Essential public services, including fire and police departments, could face sharp budget cuts due to the shortfall from lower property taxes. Orange County Fire Rescue Department via AP This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages. State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees. Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event. In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties. And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll. A looming affordable housing crunch? Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing. When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall. From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs. Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift. This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis. e9262ebde8d56524: During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: The project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using.

This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today.

In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down 10 such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity.

eeff4737bf340d02: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences. AP Photo/Lindsey WassonAs Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C. Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on. When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally. Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record. Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections. Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%. When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high. Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter. Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978. In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs. In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate. Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate. Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups. And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon. Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon. But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots. Trump’s second term During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon. On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels. Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026. Implications As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war. It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties. Michael A. 31bba1eca5b3b896: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.
A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.
